Extraordinary Tale of a Tub. A feat as novel as it was extraordinary was performed on Thursday evening in the western part of tfie Strand. A young man undertook for a wager to travel from the Adelphi Theatre to the Gulden-cross, Charing-cross on a tub. The history of all the Varieties of locomotion will not present so singular an attempt as the present, and which might he supposed, under all the circumstances, an impossibility. The start was made about half past five, and the condition was that the distance should be performed without the man getting off his wooden Bucepha. Ius more than three times. The line of road being a descent, the tub, as a matter of course, would roll down, but the difficulty was not only to keep it in a proper course, but to establish equilibrium, whilst the man was standing on the tub in its progress, and this lie did by a very rapid movement of the feet, something like the dancing on a horse's back. It appeared no easy matter to get over the crossings of tfie several streets, and at King William street the performer was some time before lie could get his vehicle in a proper direction, which, however, he accomplished and finally won the wager without assistance, and apparently without much fatigue. A large number of persons were collected during the performance, which was on a largesized ale-barrel.

The survey of the canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific had been commenced and partially completed, but discontinued for the present season in consequence of the sickness (cholera) in the province of Nicaragua. The proposed route is from San Juan de Nicaragua, (lat. 10 58 N.) up that river, (distance 130 miles,) to and through the Lake Nicaragua, distance 97 miles, to the city of Nicaragua; thence to Brietto, 16 miles, in the Gulf of Popagayo, lat 11.30N. ; whole distance, 243 miles. The survey will not be completed, until next year þÿ nor will there be any attempts to open it, until the contract is concluded between the King of Holland and the Central American government, which, it will be recollected, has been in agitation for two years past. þÿ Commercial Daily Advertiser, December 12.

( From the Commercial Advertiser, Dec: 16.) LATER FROM THE CAISADAS. By the mail of this morning we have received the following. LOWER CANADA. Correspondence of Commercial Advertiser, Montreal, Saturday, Dec. 9. The additional intelligence to what appears in this morning's Herald, that I have heard, I subjoin. I have not learned when the troops will leave tor the Grand Brule, but think it will be about Monday. The accounts from that neighborhood represent the rebels as fully determined to fight till the last for their, as they say, independence. They are very numerous, well armed, and are being well organised 1 think there is little doubt but that they will make a very fierce resistance, but 1 have no doubt they will be defeated. We have no tear of the general result. We think our volunteers are sufficient to put down all rebellion. Had the troops been defeated at St. Charles, I have not the least doubt but that the Canadians of Montreal would have butchered all the British. From the Montreal Herald, of Dec. 9. The remains of the late Lieut. Weir, of her majesty's 32d regiment, were yesterday interred with the usual military honors. All the ward and volunteer associations joined in the procession, four deep, which was certainly the most numerous we ever saw in this country. The West Ward volunteers under the command of Lieutenant Col. Maitland, lined the main street of the Quebec suburb, leaning on their arms reversed. The bands of the 32d and Royal regiments headed the procession, playing the solemn and appropriate dead

march. The pall was borne by officers of the 32d regimeet, behind whom were Sii John Cclbonie and every officer in the city who was not at the time on duty. Lieut. Weir was in the 29th year of his age. It is impossible to state how many individuals attended the funeral, but they must have numbered seven or eight thousand. The shops and counting houses in the city were closed from one to three o'clock. The windows of the houses in the streets through which the procession passed, down to Queen's Square, were crowded with females The Rev. Mr. Esson officiated at the burying ground, and in beautiful language which found a response in every breast, alluded to the untimely fate of this gallant youn : officer The interment took place in the military portion of the Scotch burying ground in Queen Street. Lord Gosford has issued a proclamation, offering $2000 reward for the discovery and appreliension of the murderers of Lieut. Weir.

TIIE C AMADAS: We have letters and papers from Montreal of the 13th instant, and advices from Toronto as late as the 11th: and we devote our columns almost exclusively to the progress of events and state of matters in those regions. The Montreal Transcript gives the following horrible account of the murder of Lieu-

l"T þÿ > Wiu u tenant Weir. The story is very different from that put forth by Mr. T. S. Brown in the Express of this morning. By the way, the Express now avows that its sometime correspondent L. M. N. and Mr. T. S. Brown, are one and the same person. After Lieut. Weir had been betrayed into the hands of the rebels, Dr. Wolfred Nelson ordered his removal from St. Denis to St. Charles. The person entrusted with this duty was Jalbert, the ex-captain of militia. þÿ that murder. Mr Wtir's arms were forced back, and his elbows made fast to each other with ropes. Thus pinioned he was placed in a cart, into which Jalbert, and another man under him, whose name we forget, also mounted, the former armed with a sword, the latter with an axe ; and they proceeded toward St. Charles. The roads were in so very bad a state that the horse became fatigued, and with difficulty continued at a foot-pace. Jalbert first ordered the man to get out and walk þÿ lie afterward got out himself þÿ and finally he made a sign to Mr. Weir, who, althougn in so helpless a condition, descended as best he might He had just reached the ground, and was steadying himself with one hand rested on the back of the cart, when Jalbert made a rush behind him, and plunged his sword into Mr. Weir's back with such violence that it transfixed Ins body. Surprised, writhing with pair, helpless! ! and influenced by the first impulse of nature, the weapon was no sooner withdrawn than Mr. Weir got under the cart, where he lay bleeding and in agony. After a short con-

ference the two assassins approached the cart and commenced a most savage and brutal attack on tlieir victim, one on each side ; the one stabbing with his sword, the other striking with his axe, as the wheel and the position of Mr. Weir gave opportunity. At length the axeman inflicted a severe wound on Mr. Weir's left side, close to the hip. þÿ Roused by tiie brutal character of the attack, and the reficction that to remain where he was. would be to die by inches, Mr. Weir crept from under the cart, and regained his legs. Seeing these wretches again advance upon him, he resorted to the only possible expedient left, and, weak as by this time he was, he raised his right leg aud made a kick at Jalbert. The man with the axe seized the advantage of the moment, and aimed a heavy blow at the left side of Mr. Weir's head. H e saw the blow coming, and instinctively raised his liand. The blow took effect across the side of the head and on a line with the temple : after cutting off all the four fingers of Mr. Weir's hand, the axe laid his skull completely open, nearly severing the top of the head. The young man then sunk upon the ground a dreadful object to behold Among the names of 25 prisoners brought to Montreal on the 12th, we observe those of Mr. Bouchetle, Dr. Kimbert, and ltodolph Desrivieres þÿ the latter a director in the I'eople's Bank. These 25 were taken at or after the affair at Moore's Corner. The names of four others, and the criminality of all the seven, are stated in the following paragraph

from the Herald of the 13th. Bouchette is the late editor of the Quebec Liberal, At has taken a very active part in the recent measures of his party. We are told that both he and Kimbert held commands at Missisquoi. Kimbert was also deeply implicated in the first movement at Longuenil þÿ Desrivieres, Marchessault and Boucher Belle-

ville, were all active and prominent at St. Charles. Jalbert was at St I 'enis, and we believe at St. Charles too; and, more than that, is understood to have had the chief hand in the murder of Lieut. Weir. Roi, if not actually the most guilty of those concerned in the murder of poor Chartrand, was at least the man who gave the word of command to lire upon him, and must therefore be considered as among those most deeply implicated in

We stated, a few days since, that Mr T. S. Brown is a native of New Brunswick, and not of Vermont or M assaehusolts, as has been alleged in various quarters. The following, from the Herald, shows that we were correct ; " Mr. T. S. Brown, to the honor of the Americans on either side of the line, be it said, is not an American by birth, but a native ol New Brunswick, who has spent some years ol his earlier life in Vermont. He has been many years in Canada. The object which has induced him, as much as possible, to pass hiinsell off" as a Vermonter, is easily guessed.'' We believe that .Mr. Brown resided some time in Halifax, N. S., where he married a young lady, who lived but a short time alter giving birth to a daughter, now about seven years of age.

Burlington, Vermont, Deo. 12, 1£3'7. I wrote you in great haste yesterday in reply to your letter of the 8th instant ; and in compliance with my promise, 1 write you again to-dav, to give you more at length the result of the inquiries I have made upon the subject of the late struggle of the Canadians for independence. Jn saying late, I think I use the word advisedly, as a conversation with Mr. Brown, who arrived in today's stage from Swanton, has fully confirmed me, and I may add others, w ho were present at the conversation, in my previous opinions, that, whether right or wrong in their object, the Canadians have been altogether premature in their attempt at revolution. Mr. Brown effected his ( scape to Vermont with great difficulty. He informs me that he and Dr. IVelson, u ho, he insists, are alone responsible for the. operations on the part of the Canadians, at St. Denis and St. Charles, finding that they were wholly unable to meet the force which had been sent against them, under Colonel Core, advised the men under their command to disperse and go home, while themselves, under the direction of a guide employed for that purpose, sought their way, through the woods, to Ve rmont. Indeed, Mr. Brown himself publicly admits, that the rising was not intended to take place till next year, and that, at this moment, the Canadians are not assembled for resistanee nor for any purpose, in any part of the province. The truth most assuredly is, that the whale affair has proved an utter abortion. The

Canadians have altogether mistaken their strength þÿ or rather their leaders have mistaken their influence. For it is most certain, that there is a very widespread opinion among those who have been urged to measures of open resistance, that their leaders have deserted them. Indeed, such was the feeling of indignation at the unsuccessful issue of the affair at St. Charles, that Mr. Brown, as ho himself admits, was actually, lor some time, detained under arrest by his own men. But, however that may be, the people, lately in arms, have returned to their homes, while their leaders have fled the country.

P. R. We have a letter from Montreal, dated the 13th, which announces the capture of Wolfred Nelson. He had just been brought in, with a Canadian and Indian, who had been his guides. On the morning of the 13th detachments of the 1st Royals, and of the 32nd and 88rd regiments, marched for St. Eustache, the Lake of the Two Mountains and Grand Brule þÿ The insurgent force at the latter place was reported to be large. The detachments above mentioned, with six field pieces, the volunteer rifle corps, and a troop of horse, commanded by Sir John Colborne in person, were to make the attack on Friday last, assisted by the Glengarry militia, from the upper province. Such arrangements were made as would ensure the capture of till the insurgents, if they held their ground until the arrival of the troops. The force of the expedition was about 2000.

UPPER CANADA. We have but one paper from the province þÿ the Kingston Chronicle of the 1 3th instant, containing advices from Toronto of the 11th. The number of volunteers assembled at Toronto on the 7th, was about 2500, who marched under the command of Sir Francis Head against the insurgents, who had taken possession of Montgomery's tavern. From this they were speedily dislodged by a single shot from a brass gun, and took up a position on a hill ; hut fled on the nearer approach of the volunteers. The tavern was then burned, the horses of the insurgents, about 20 in number, having first been taken from the stables. The insurgents appear to have made scarcely a show of resistance. About 30 of them were made prisoners. Volunteers were pouring into Kingston from the surrounding district, for the defence of that cov in case of need. The number under arms lor that purpose on the 13th, was about 520, besides a strong nightly patrol. þÿ Seventy-five of the 520 were in Fort Henry, the second in command being Captain Macfai lane, editor of i lie Kingston Chronicle. On the 11th i list. Sir Francis Head issued his proclamation, summoning the provincial Parliament to meet, for the actual despatch of business, on the 21st.

We have prepared a full account of the extraordinary proceedings at Buffalo and elsewhere in this slate, and intended to publish it in this day's paper ; but a press of advertisements, and oilier matters requiring immediate attention, compels us to defer these articles until our next. We can only make room for the subjoined letter, by which it appears that the citizens of Buffalo, under the auspices of Mr. William Lyon Mackenzie, are actually preparing to invade the soil of Upper Canada, in violation of the laws as well of our own republic as of nations. Correspondence of Commercial Advertiser. Eagle Hotel, Buffalo, ) Dec. 13, 1837. \ I have just arrived here, and find all bustle and excitement Mc'Kenzic is here. I have just seen him. Last night he addressed a very large meeting, in the theatre. There was great excitement ; and a great many volunteered to go to Canada with him. Placards were posted up all round the city today, asking assistance in any shape, and this evening the following placard appears on every post and corner in this vicinity.

From the New York Advertiser, Dec: 23 LATEST FROM LOWER CANADA. Close of the Expedition to Grand Brule. þÿ The Montreal Herald of the 16th brings the following account from Grand Brule, where the insurrection has been put down without more bloodshed " At eight o'clock yesterday morning the troops marched from St Eustache, and reached Grand ; Brule about noon Previous to leaving St. Eustache, a flag of truce had been received by Sir John ; but that did not interfere with his preconcerted operations. Every house within a mile of the village of Grand Brule had a white pocket handkerchief, stuck on a stick, exhibited from a window, to give evidence of the peaceful intentions of its inmates. On arriving opposite Girouard's house, the general halted, and made it his head quarters. Immediately opposite were about 250 Canadians drawn up rank and file, a few of them holding up white handkerchiefs on sticks. þÿ They exhibited as pitiful an appearance as could possibly be imagined, and surrendered themselves unconditionally. In Girouard's house several papers were found, containing lists of his several companies and various other matters connected with Ins mad projects. A person named Majore, one of the prisoners at St. Eustache, who was wounded in the side by an officer with his sword, says that at the beginning of the action, the rebels amounted to nearly a thousand. A considerable number of them fled as soon as they heard the first discharge of crtillery, and it is conjectured that from one hundred and fifty

to two hundred were killed by the military, or perished in the flames. 7'he nurnbei of corpses in the church-yard and the nuns' gardens is twenty-eight, and from thirty to forty individuals were killed in the brushwood in attempting to retreat. þÿ When the troops arrived at St. Eustache, Girod, Peltier, and a few others left to bring up reinforcements, as they said, but, as a matter of course, they never returned. 2'hey went to grand Brule and the North Ki ver, but were not successful in either place in raising troops, and they are now supposed to be skulking about the woods. The number prisoners taken at St. Eustache is 123, of and the number of wounded about 20, of whom 4 have died since they were placed in the hospital. The troops lost one man killed and five men were wounded, though not seriously. þÿ The daring exposure of his person by B. A. Gugy, Esq , uufortunatcly was taken advantage of by the enemy, lie is wounded in two places, but was doing well yesterday at two o'clock. On Thursday evening the village of St. Eustachc presented a heart-rending appeariuice, the whole of the lower portion being

3>Air3X TaStMSNErtSZ ®»<0JHKftira«3 jv.733. one sheet of lurid flame. It is supposed that about fifty houses have been burnt, and nothing now is left of them but stone walls or solitary chimneys. We understand that the prisoners are to he brought into Montreal. Sir John and the troops were to occupy Grand Brule last night, and proceed this day to St, Seliolastique and St. Therese, and then home. It is supposed that the houses of Jacob Barcelo and Girouard would be burnt by the troops previous to their departure."

St. Benoit, Grand Brut', ) December 15, 1837. ) My Dear Sir þÿ 1 have to acquaint you that a division of the Queen's troops, under my command, entered St. Eustache yesterday, driving out of that village about 1200 rebels that had occupied it lor ten days, and committed every outrage, plundering the whole country in this neighborhood, arid destroying the property of the loyalists. We marched to,St. Benoit, (Grand Brule,) this morning. The rebel army have laid down their arms, and have dispersed. Yours faithfully, J. COLRORNE. J. Buchanan, Esq British Consul, N. Y.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, December 21. STATE OF VERMONT. A PROCLAMATION. BY THE (JOVEKNOR. It is well known to my fellow citizens that disturbances have broken out in the neighboring province of Lower Canada, which have resulted in bloodshed. The head of the provincial Government has issued his proclamation, declaring martial law in the district of Montreal. This state of things necessarily changes the relations which have heretofore existed between the inhabitants of this state and that province, and the possibility that any, through the influence of ardent feelings, may be betrayed into acts of unauthorized interference, induces me to call the attention of my fellow citizens to the subject. With the kingdom of Great Britain we are in a state of profound peace. We have treaties with that government which it is our duty, and I trust our desire, to fulfil to the letter. It is obvious that as a nation we have no right to intermeddle with the constitution of any neighboring power While as republicans we prefer that form of government under which it is our happiness to live, a decent regard for the opinion of others, will prevent all dictation as to the form of their government. Principles which have been admitted for ages, forbid all national interference unless in the character of allies, and it is scarcely necessary to add that individuals should not do that which the government cannot þÿ must not do. It has been represented to me, that in some few instances arms have been furnished, and hostile forces organized within this state. No

one can be ignorant of the consequences of such a state of things if allowed. Such forces may be repelled, and our territory be made tire theatre of active warfare. This is not to be tolerated for a moment, and every good citizen will appreciate the importance of rebuking all such acts as may tend to produce it. That comity which binds nations to each other, condemns all interference in their intestine broils, and the laws of Congress are explicit in their denunciation, subjecting those who improperly interfere to heavy penalties and imprisonment. Under these circumstances, and with tliese feelings, I have thought it my duty to issue this my Proclamation, cautioning my fellow citizens against all acts that may subject them to penalties, or in any way comproniit the government. Our first duty is to our own government ; and tle greatest benefit we can confer on the world is by giving them a perfect example in the action of that government. With other nations our conduct should lie regulated by the principles of an enlarged and enlightened philanthropy. in war we may treat them as enemies ; but in peace they are to he regarded as friends. In the present posture of affairs our duty is manifest þÿ that of a strict þÿneutrality neither lending such aid to either as would be inconsistent with that character, nor denying the rights of Itospilality to either, so long as tliev are within our borders, and maintain the character of quiet and peaceable citizens Mv fellow citizens will appreciate the feel-
ings by which I am actuated, The nation's

3&AST3K T2BOT3W1DJ131R mEHUEmilSms AT33< honor cannot be confided to better hands than our own. Their zeal in the cause of liberty was never doubted. It is only necessary to caution them against such interference with the rights of others as might jeopardize the peace of our country. Given under my band this 13lh day of December, A. D 1837, and of the Independence of the United States the sixtysecond. S. H. JENISON. By the Governor, G. B. Manser, Secretary.

Yesterday I had the pleasure of receiving vour's of the 27th ultimo, and am happy to give you correct information, as far as I am able, of the passing events in our province. With regard to the grievances of the Canadians, they have, in fact, none. þÿ They pay no tuxes whatever þÿ their religion, their language, and their laws are guaranteed to them þÿ and they are naturally a peaceable and hospitable people. But the whole secret is they are an ignorant race, and being ignorant, the priests have encouraged this state of ignorance ; they therefore feel themselves inferior to persons from the old country, from the U. S., and think they are degraded. They wish to get rid of this evil bv either driving out or massacring every English inhabitant of this province, and establishing a French republic, with Mr. Papineau as their President. Providentially, a collision took place, which brought on the rebellion a month or six weeks earlier than Mr. Papineau intended it Their plans were therefore not mature, but as it was, the excitement among the Canadians was very great. I could not have believed that so great an excitement could have been produced. But in addition to the picture before them of a French republic, the great temptation was held out. that they were immediately to march upon Montreal, which they expected to take with very little difficulty, and to plunder the city. If this had been effected, the scenes of the French revolution would have been enacted over again

Some of the Canadians who have taken the lead in this rebellion are as cruel and blood thirsty as even Robespierre and othcrst who figured in France ; but God, in his providence, has defeated their schemes, and prevented such a dreadful evil to come upon us. The accounts you have seen in the Montreal papers of the march of troops, and the attack upon St. Charles, which was the stronghold of the Canadians, and where the latter were completely routed are perfectly correct. All that part of the country between Chamhly and Sorel, upward of forty miles in a straight line, is, as you well know, one complete village, and is the most valuable part of the province. It has always been a great wheat country. St Charles is situated nearly in the centre of this line, along the Chambly river, which forms a junction with the St. Lawrence at Sorel. Rebellion in all that part of the country is crushed ; and Air. Papineau is said to have passed Mount Johnson last Friday, on his way to the States. You will probably see him in New York. My opinion is that he will pass the residue of his days in France. Civil war, or rather rebellion, is still raging at the back of us, to the North. Before the St Charles affair was settled, we were in a state of great anxiety. For a few days, we were daily in expectation of an attack on Montreal and even in our city were hun- , dreds of Canadians, armed, ready to join the rebels the moment they arrived. But now we have not the least apprehension of an at-

tack. We are all organized. Every able bodied man is a soldier. Scarcely any thing is attended to here hut drilling. As soon as the winter sets in, I believe Sir John Colborne intends to despatch a party of troops <o the back of the island of Montreal, to at-
Our correspondent alludes to the country in the vicinity of the two Mountains, of Grand JBrule, &c. þÿ Com. Adv.

mmomasms AT'J3, tack the disaffected in that part of the country ; and then I think rebellion will be at an end þÿ at all eveuts, for the present. Future events we must leave. Very much will depeud on what the home government may do- My opinion is, there has been too much concession to meet the wishes of Mr. Papineau. Look aj the removal of one of our judges from the bench, on ex-parte evidence of the House of Assembly, and removing from the office of attorney general, a lawyer, who is acknowledged by all parties, to he the ablest jurist in the province, by a simple address to that effect from the House of Assembly. Papineau well knew, that as long as this man, (James Stewart,) held that office, the Canadians would not be permitted to make the least attempt to rebel. You have long known Mr Stewart, and you can bear me out in my assertion. In Montreal the Canadians were drilling for six weeks, frequently parading the streets at night, with the tri-colored ffag, and marching through the town every Sunday afternoon þÿ this 1 have seen And although the governor was made acquainted with all these facts, no attempt was made to stop it. In Sir John Colboriie, the commander of the forces, we have every tiling we could wish lor.

We have not waited to receive our whole file of papers from the Post Office, the mail being immensely large; but having obtained the one containing Her þÿMajesty Speech s on meeting her first Parliament, we made the best of our way to our Office in order that this þÿevening s paper may convey to our readers a document, which, though usually rather vapid and uninteresting, politicians are always anxious to see. The character of the speech is one of caution and conciliation, and deals rather in generalities In the House of Commons Lord Leveson moved the address in answer to Her Majesty s gracious speech, alluded to its conciliatory character, and deprecated any thing like angry discussion on an occasion when unanimity was so desirable. Mr. Gibson Gkaig seconded the address ; Mr Wakley, ultra Radical, moved an amendment, the object of which was to remedy the omissions in the speech, to which he adverted ; maintaining that the defects of the Reform Act ought to be corrected, and proposing to pledge the House to the consideration of measures for the extension of the elective franchise, and the security of its free exercise by the adoption of vote by ballot, and by shortening the duration of parliament Sir Wm Moi.es worth seconded the amendment, and denounced the Reform Act as an entire and complete failure Lord John Russell opposed the amendment, w hich

lie considered would be tantamount to a repeal of the Reform Act. He would not deny the right of the House to originate such measures as those propounded in the amendment, but he should resist them as a violation ol the engagement which accompanied the Reform Act, and as seeking to disturb a final measure. Sir Robert Peel observed, that many occasions would present themselves hereafter for discussing the various subjects touched upon in the Royal þÿ Speech, but he should oppose the amendment, as he should resist all efforts to alter the Reform Act ; and in common with the noble Lord (J. Russell) he should resist this perpetual desire of change. With respect to the result of the last general election, he did not consider it so much as matter of party triumph, as of proof that the country was opposed to this continued agitation and restless demand for variety. Mr. Wakely pressed his amendment, for which 20 members voted, and against it þÿ509 majority in favour of the original address, 489. The amendments attempted to be made to an Address drawn up by Ministers, shews a schism in tire liberal ranks. Jt forced -Lord John Rijsseli,, the ministerial leader in the House of Commons, to throw himself on the Conservatives for protection. 1 1 is Lordship has now declared that he considered the questions of the Ballot, Universal Suffrage, and Triennial Parliaments, as virtually repealing the Reform Act, and that he would rather reign than assist in carrying them. I bis raised a great ferment among the Ultra-

Liberals who declare that it will be fatal to the Melbourne Ministry. Now we think the Ministry stands firmer than ever, for they seem veering round to Conservatism. Lord John þÿRussell speech s on the Address exhibits a firm and uncompromising purpose to maintain the stability of the fundamental principles of the Constitution The Church, wo venture to hope, is safe. Lord John Russell has declared that the attempt on the Church has signally failed, and that there was

no chance of success against it. The late elections have brought his Lordship, we dare say, to this conclusion ; for the people have decidedly declared themselves in favour of the support and maintainance of the Church. A very cursory view of the papers, has enabled us to say that things look cheering. On Wednesday we hope to present our readers with a better summary of intelligence. >»< HOUSE OF LORDS, November 20.

The Irish blunder is sui generis ; and it is not only of a class by itself, but it is of the best class. It always puzzles, which inere clownishness does not; hut it always amuses by its oddity, its novelty, and its humour. This talent goes through all ranks. From the New York Co mmercial Advertiser, January 3, 1838. IMPORTANT INTELLIGENCE. Another Northern mail lias just arrived, and has furnished us with the following important intelligence The Upper Canada Gazette Extraordinary brings us the message of Sir Francis Head, at the opening of Parliament It relates of course, almost exclusively to the recent events in the province, and those now in progress on our side. Of the latter Governor Head speaks in strong but calm and impressive language. þÿ prisoners He expresses forcibly the surprise and regret with which he has found the province entrusted to him by his sovereign, invaded by people a with whom that sovereign is at peace, and to whom no provocation has been given. From this part of the message we quote the fol owing : þÿ in la informed that Americans from various quarters are hastening from the interior to join this standard of avowed plunder and revolt that cannon and arms are publicly þÿ proceeding there þÿ and tinder these circumstances, it becomes my painful duly to inform you. that without having offered to the United States the smallest provocation- -without having entertained the slightest previous doubt of the sincerity of American alliance, the in habitants of this provinc may in a few days be called upon by me to defend their lives, their properties, and their liberties, from an attack by American citizens, which, with no desire to offend, 1 must pronounce to be unparalleled in the history of the world. Gov. Head declares that he feels no anxiety for the result, and adds þÿ þÿ The peaceful

inhabitants of Upper Ganada will not be left to defend their country alone, for they belong to an empire which does not suffer its subjects to be injured with impunity ; and if a national war which it rests with the American Government to avert, should be the unhappy' consequence of an intolerant invasion of our freedom, the civilized world, while it sympathizes with our just cause, will view feelings of astonishment and abhorrence this attempt of a body of American citizens treacherously to attack and plunder in a moment of profound peace, their oldest, their most intimate, and their most natural þÿally. In conclusion, Sir Francis says that, firmly anticipating from the American people a noble vindication of their government and institutions, and holding it but just to allow them a reasonable time to do so, he has communicated with the governor of New York and the British minister at Washington ; and while awaiting their replies, has reinforced the militia by a strong corps of observation on the frontier, and made arrangements for a levy en masse of the militia should their services unhappily be required. Department of State, Washington, Dec. 7, 1837. Sir . þÿ In the course of the contest which has commenced in a part of the territory of Great Britain, between portions of the population and the Government, some of our citizeus may, from their connection with the settlers, and from their love of enterprise and desire of change, be induced to forget their duty to their own Government, and its obligations to foreign powers. It is the fixed determination of the President faithfully to discharge, so far as his power extends, all the obligations of this Government, and that obligation especially which requires that we shall abstain, under every temptation, from intermeddling with the domestic disputes of other nations. You are, therefore, earnestly enjoined to be attentive to all movements of a hostile character, contemplated or attempted within your district, and to prosecute, without discrimination, all violators of those laws of the United States, which have been enacted to preserve peace with foreign powers, and to fulfil all the obligations of our treaties with them. I am, sir, Your obedient servant, JOHN FORSYTH. Nathaniel S. Benton, Esq. THE EMPEROR OF RUSSIA AT WUSNESEMSK. The Emperor arrived at Wosnesensk on the noth of August ; the Empress on the 5th of September. A magnificent evening favored her entrance. The Emperor had ridden out in the morning to meet her, and w hen, at six in the evening, she presented herself at the gates of the city, a brilliant staff of general officers, covered with orders, feathers, and embroideries, crowded around her carriage. The Emperor escorted her on horseback, while the eager multitude, and the moving procession galloping along the boulevard, formed a magnificent coup ifail In another moment, as if by enchantment, a general illumination was seen throughout the whole city, and in the square in front of the palace assembled the performers of the most majestic music that I have ever heard. I do not speak merely of the 1500 musicians, who, with perfect precision, executed several favorite airs þÿ the effect was very fine certainly, but such an effect may easily be produced elsewhere ; but what made tlie liveliest impression on me was the vocal part of this colossal concert. þÿ Wore than a thousand young men, the sons of the military colonists, soldiers themselves by birth, sang most admirably our Russian M God save the þÿKing, national melody a which the talent of Lvof, Aid-de Camp to the Emperor, has rendered highly popular among us. The effect of a thousand judiciously selected voices swelling into a chorus was most sublime, and more than once a thrill of admiration evidently pervaded the surrounding

crowd. A simple but imposing ceremony terminated th) evening. Suddenly these soldiers, musicians, singers, and spectators, with uncovered heads and inclined bodies, were seen listening to a short prayer which lose from among them. Though the priest was seen

To my travelling companions, little familiarised with these patriarchal manners, the mighty tumult, and the enthusiasm of loyalty, subsiding before the voice of prayer, was an object at onec of interest and admiration. We asked ourselves whether, in any other city of Europe, where the bustle of a festival had united thousands of men, the feeble voice of a priest would have been powerful enough to appease at once the tumult of the crowd, and make every one bend down in homage to religion.

It is not my intention to attempt a description of the skilful manoeuvres of which Wosnesensk is at every instant the animated theatre i military men agree in saying that these operations are beautitully executed, which is the less astonishing, as the soldiers here assembled have for the most part grown old under their colours. 1 was myself present only at the general review of cavalry, on the 7 ill of September. Thirty-six regiments were drawn up in four lines on the plain with a numerous artillery behind them, forming a fifth line The Emperor passed along each line ; the Hereditary Grand Duke, the Grand Duke Michael, and a multitude of general officers accompanied his Majesty. where fact that, in tins country, It is a well known the anny includes so many fine men, tlie Emperor is considered to be the best-looking horseman in the whole empire. The Empress accompanied by her daughter, a young and beautiful princess, also passed along the line in an elegant blue caleche. The foreign officeis who had been invited, had tlie honor of serving as an escort to the Empress, for whom the chief honors of ibe fete were reserved. W lien the troops defiled, the Emperor placed himselt at their head, and gave the word of command in a loud and audible voice ; on passing his august consort he saluted her with Ins sword, and then placed himself by her side. It occupied four hours before thousand troops had defiled. Fifty the whole of the men of tlie finest cavalry composed the corps d'armee

united under the command of Count de Witt. Next to the variety and beauty of the uniforms, nothing struck us more than the fine appearance of the horses, the color scrupulously matched for each regiment ; the a haunonious effect of this, when so large bony ol men are assembled, must be seen to be understood The review of infantry took place on the 8th ol September, in which 28 battalions of fine old troops participated ; and here 1 think it tight to tell you what appeared most to strike the foreign officers present. Above all, to sec united under the command ol one man, and obeying his orders, a mass ol regular cavalry, such us ihe largest armies, not even the grand army of Napoleon, in 1812, ever beheld united upon one point No less deserving of intesest was the sight of these 15.000 horsemen, accompanied by a formidable artillery, passing without confusion from one order to another, operating changes of front, and each arm preserving its proper place, and arriving at the exact point assigned to it, in front of the supposed enemy ; the light cavalry in the van next the cuirassiers, and as a reserved corps 00 squadrons of dragoons, a particularly line body of troops. þÿ The foreign officers all agreed admiring in the mobility of those musses, the beauty ol the ensemble, the perfection of liver details; above all, they noticed the admirable coup d'cnl of the Emperor, and the facility with which he put this innumerably cavalry into motion. The Russian Dragoons are a creation of

the Emperor hi./vself, or at least tlie realisation of ideas -long meditated on by his Majesty, who lias formed of them at once an excellent body of cavalry, ready to act at the same t ine as a formidably infantry. They require only two minutes and a half to be ready to fight on foot, or to re-mount their horses. Imagine eight complete battalions debouching suddenly from behind a curtain ot artillery when the enemy expects to be opposed only by cavalry, and you may suppose tlie effect which a good general would be but by few, his voice pierced to the soul þÿ able to produce with so powerful and flexible a reserve. At the same time that the organization of this immense colonised cavalry was going on care was taken to form a nursery for noncommissioned officers. These arc readily found among the children of the soldiers, brought up from infancy in military habits, receiving sufficiently good theoretic and most excellent practical instruction. On beholding this þÿremarkable ensemble it is impossible not to render homage to the enlightened zeal of Count de Witt, the commandant of all the forces assemble at Wosnesensk ; but his merit is more correctly

appreciated w'hen we of ate cial administration these military colonies told llrat the finanhas furnished, out of Ids savings, nil the sums necessary to the maintenance and displacement of the troops: We have now returned to Odessa. Tomorrow, ( 1 7th Sept.) tlie Emperor is expected to arrive here. A. DemiUoif.

SPECIAL MESSAGE or TriE Governor of New York. To the Legislature : I received last evening, after my annual message was prepared, information of an occurrence which 1 hasten to communicate to you. The territory of this state has been invaded, and some of our citizens murdered, by an armed force from the Province of Upper Canada. By the documents accompanying this communication, it will be perceived that the st am-boat Caroline, owned by one of our citizens, while K intr at Sublessor on the Niagara river, within ihe limits of this state, on the night of the 29tn of December last, was forcibly seized bv a party seventy eigh- of or ty armed men in boats, which came from, and returned to. the Canadian shore. The crew and other persons in this steam boat amounting to thirty three, were suddenly attacked at mid night, after they had retired to repose, and probably more than one third of them wantonly massacred. The boat was

detached from the wharf to which it had been secured, set on fire, taken into the middle of the river, and by the force of the current carried over the Niagara Falls. Twelve of the persons who were on board of it are missing, and there is ground to fear that they were killed by the invaders in their attack upon it, or perished in its descent over the cataract. Of these who escaped from the boat, one was killed on the wharf, and several others were wounded. 1 am warranted in assuring you, that the authorities not only of this state, but of the United States, have felt an anxious solicitude to maintain the relations of peace and strict neutrality with the British provinces of Upper and Lower Canada at all times since the commencement of the civil disturbances therein and have in all respects done what was incumbent upon them to do to sustain these relations. The occurrence to which I have alluded, is an outrage that has not been provoked by any act done, or duty neglected, by the Government, or of this State or of the Union. If it should appear that this boat was intended to be used for the purpose of keeping up an intcrcouise between this state and Navy Island, which is now held by an I lived ten years amongst us, five of those lie assemblage persons of in defiance of the Canadian government, this circumstance would furnish no justification for the hostile invasion of our territory jand the destruction of the lives of our citizens. The general government is entrusted with
the maintenance of our foreign relations, and will undoubtedly take the necessary steps to redress the wrong and sustain the honor of the country.

H>AJT32K T33TaiTJ>33K BBOWKBaSroS A733» Though 1 have received no official information of the fact, I have good reason to believe that the local authorities of this state have taken prompt and efficient means, not only protect to our soil from further invasion, but to repress any retaliative measures of aggression which our citizens under the impulse of deeply excited and indignant feelings, might rashly resolve to adopt ; and that the patriotic militia in the vicinity of the scene of the outrage, fiave 'obeyed with alacrity the call which has been made upon them for these purposes. It will probably be necessary for this state to keep up a military force for the protection of our citizens and the maintenance of peacei until an opportunity is given to the general government to interpose with its power. In that event, 1 apprehend that it will be necessary for you to provide by law for the payment and oiaintenance of such forces as the occasion may require. I shall doubtless receive within a short time, official information of what the local authorities have done, and shall be better enabled to form an opinion of what will be necessary on the part of this state to preserve our rights and the public tranquility. 1 shall then communicate further with you on the subject, and suggest such matters in relation to it as may require your consideration. W. L. MAUCY. Albany, Jan. 2, 1838.

From the Port of Spain Gazette, þÿDec br. 12. Consecration of the Rev. Dr. Smith as Bishop of Agna, The appointment of Dr. Smith to act as coadjutor of Dr. Mae. Donnell, gave general satisfaction. The foimer Gentleman has

has been Vicar of Fort of Spain, and his disposition is so amiable, that all here entertain sanguine hopes lie will emulate the Episcopal virtues of Dr. Mac Donnell. On Sunday the 10th of December, the imposing ceremony of Consecration took place at the Catholic Cathedral, Fort of Spain. þÿ On this occasion there were more than 3,000 persons in the Church, and a vast concourse of persons outside. The 89th Regiment at-

tended as a guard of honor; þÿ the Corps of the Trinidad Artillery were also assembled on this occasion. About 9 þÿo clock in the morning the body of the Cathedral became crowded, and from the Gallery in which our Reporter was to have been seated, the congregated multitude below had a beautiful appearance The interior of this noble Cathedral has a grand effect, although the whole building lias been erected in no order of Architecture, and can scarcely be said to be in pure Gothic style ; yet so stately and elegantly has it been constructed to accord with the climate, that it wants but a more suitable grand Altar to be all that art could require. It is undoubtedly one of the noblest buildings in this part of the world 'Fhe fitting up of the interior for the service of this day, did credit to the taste of the Gentlemen concerned in it. About 25 minutes past 9, his Excellency the Lieutenant Governor and Staff arrived, attended by Brigadier General Feschier, and most of the Fublic Officers. He was met by the Bishop of Olympus and a numerous train of Clergy, wdio conducted him to the grand Altar, where he received the honors of the Representative of Royalty. For many reasons, it is not in our power to give a detailed description of the entire of this imposing ceremony, w hich was mingled and blended with the High Mass ; þÿ the effect of the whole had that striking, awful, and magnificent effect, with which the Church of Rome so well know's how to invest her solemn services. The appearance of the Consecrating

Bishop surrounded by his Priests, Acolites, Cross and Incense Bearers, while standing near or seated beside the Grand Altar, with his magnificent Robe®, resplendent Mitre and Crozier, attended by the Assistant Bishops and Deacons, covered with Robes of Gold Tissue, the Bishop elect while either prostrated before the Altai during the chanting of the Litany of the Saints, or when invested with his Mitre and Crozier, he walked down the Aisle of the Church, giving the people his Episcopal benediction, were strikingly grand. A long and eloquent Sermon was preached on this occasion by the Reverend Mr. Mac Donnell, a name-sake of Lis Lordship of Olympus. During the Mass, Eyrie E/ieson and the Credo, from þÿWeber s Mass, in G, Major were beautifully sung, by a party of Ladies and Gentlemen, in the Gallery, accompanied by the Musical Amateurs of this Town, the Artillery Band, and the Band of the 89th. When the newly consecrated Bishop, raised his arms to give his blessing to the flock confided to his care, all the guns of the garrison, with those of the regiment of artillery, fired several rounds, and thus closed the most solemn and sublime religious ceremonies, ever witnessed in the islands of America. The Mass, Consecration and sermon took up four hours. We have to apologize for the meagerness of this account ; the imperfection of our report was occasioned by the fact of our reporter having been deprived of his scat, through what, he is willing to believe was, a mistake.

From our Special Correspondent. Albany, Jan. 3. 1838, Dear Sir : þÿ As you may suppose, all sorts of rumors are rife and current here ; hut there is one lately reached us by a gentleman direct from Buffalo, to which considerable credence is jriven. It is neither more nor less than that an attack has been made on Navy Island, on New Year's Day, bv the British regular troops and loyalist volunteers, headed by Colonel þÿMo Nab, and that under cover of a severe canonading from the Chippewa side, they finally effected a landing Some severe fighting is said to have taken place, which resulted in the loyalists obtaining possession, and remaining masters of the Island It is further stated that they came down the stream hugging the shore of Grand Island close, and so effected a landing on that part of Navy Island, immediately covered by the east end of Grand Island ! Such is the rumor þÿ w hich I send to you for what it is worth. We are all excitement here, but this excitement does not manifest itself in any particular outburst of public feeling ; but rather in a silent, sullen, settled determination of vengeance, for the atrocious act of butchery recently perpetrated. In all parts of the city, young, active, hardy, and daring men may be seen scouring up their rifles, and setting their shot guns in order. There is no longer any

þÿ concealment of their intentions ; no alleged hunting or shooting party." They openly state that they mean to take dinner in Toronto in 2 or 3 weeks. A large meeting of citizens was held here yesterday relative to 'Canada and the late outrage, threat excitement prevailed, and Mr. L F. Allen, of Buf falo, was sent for from the House of Assembly. He came þÿ made a short speech, and recommended calm and deliberative conduct till further particulars should arrive as to the behavior of the British authorities After which the meeting adjourned till to-morrow, Thursday. þÿJlurfee sfuneral was attended by nearly 3000 people In coming into town this alternoon, I met at least from 20 to 30 men, armed in various way's, and in groupes of various numbers, taking up the þÿ line of þÿmarch for the scene of action I send this by a special messenger. In haste. On Saturday morning last a correspondence took place between the Distict Attorney of the U. States (by the hand of Judge þÿMc Lane of Buffalo) and Col. Allan þÿMe Nab, , he British Commander of the Niagara frontier This was a few hours previous to the outrage on the Caroline, and our readers will perceive that the British officer promptly disavows all intentions of infringing our neutrality, while he raps his correspondent pretty severely on the knuckles respecting our gttasi-neutrality þÿ that sort of impartiality which is all on one side. As a soldier and a cntleman, we are bound to believe Colonel þÿIc Nab professions, s and entertain not the

slightest doubt that the whole affair proe.eeded from that embittered partizan feeling of personal grudge which is always the concomitant of border hostilities. Buffalo, 2!fth Dec. 1837. How shamefully and wickedly that neutrality has been and is daily violated, we need not tell our readers ; nor have they vet to learn how feebly & inefficiently our government has acted in the performance of I century, and they are becoming serious its duty. Not a word has been spoken by the Globe þÿ the recognized organ of the federal government þÿ and the Argus, the official paper of our own slate, has openly encouraged those violations of national faith and of our ! his proclamation of neutrality, and if the civil own explicit laws, which arc at this moment ripening to maturity the elements of a war against ns by Great Britain ; a war, too. in which no particle of justice will be with us, &. which every consideration of principle and interest at once requires us to avoid, and en- | supplied with arms from our own arsenals, lists against us the judgment and tire feelings of all other civilized nations. Mr. Garrow was sent to the West expressly for the purpose of enforcing tltc laws. þÿ W ell, if he has no power to fulfil his commission, whose duty is it to give him power t Doubtless the prerogative rests either with Congress, or the legislature of New York. þÿ Both these bodies are now in session, and
unless they wish to get into a war with England, the) can't be too quick in adopting efficient measures to prevent encroachments upour Northern neighbors, by expiditions

Tim Canada War þÿ Referring the reader to the extracts which we publish in another column, we are constrained to remark that what is called the Canada war, is no longer an insurrection, but a war the sinews and aliment of which are chiefly supplied from the United States. There is no doubt that our neutrality has been frequently violated, in more instances than one perhaps we should say, is violated continually. The Courier <3f - Enquirer. The affair of Navy Island is assuming a very serious aspect. The position of the insurgents is undoubtedly strong, their number is daily increasing, and their supplies of arms, ammunition, and all the sinews of war, receive daily augmentation. There is no doubt that the state of feeling along our frontier, threatens to implicate us in most unfortunate difficulties with England. A rumor was in circulation yesterday, that the British minister had demanded his passports. This we can hardly believe to be true ; hut if our Government do not call out some volunteer corps, enforce obedience to the laws and compel our citizens to respect our neutrality, we should not be surprised if Mr. Fox should feel it incumbent on him to close his mission. It is the duty of the federal Government to make use of all the means in its power, to compel obedience to our treaty stipulations and our national obligations. On this subject at least, tlieie can he no difference of opinion

between all right minded men. The Gazette. It has been with a single eye to the nation, al faith and honor that we have ever said a word on the subject of the contest in Canada. We do not ourselves see anything in the complaints made by the Canadians themselves, or the still more zealous declamations put forth for them in the United Stntes, to warrant their revolt from the mother country. We may be mistaken, however. It is barely possible that they are the injured and oppressed people that they are represented ; but it is not possible to mistake cither the ridiculousness, the wickedness or the impolicy the of movements making in their behalf among American citizens They are the grossest outrages t hat civilization has witnessed for a
enough for actual alarm. (Jur Government is not doing its duty, whatever may be said of it. Why is it that the President has hot issued

powei to enforce it is insufficient for the purpose, why is not the militia put in requisition on the frontiers ? Is it to be said of us that an army can he raised within our own territory, for the invasion of a neutral country þÿ

and provisioned from our own store houses, with perfect impunity ? We have no disposition to hunt up arguments for a declaration of war against us by a foreign Government, hut we have no hesitation in saying, that half the provocation on the part of Great Britain would rouse the citizens of the United States into one unanimous feeling of exasperation. þÿ We should he willing go to to war at once. Was there ever such fatuity as upon por- is a tion of our þÿpopulation such wretched, reckless, and unmitigated fatuity ? We perceive that the Buflalonians are in a perfect hurricaoe «J ire at the bare suicioit

that some Canadians had innded on Grand þÿIsland and even the district attorn< y sent to the frontiers expressly for the purpose of checking the effervescence of our American thirst for Canada invasion, has given countenance and encouragement to that feeling. þÿ Where sleeps the sensibility to the in' asion of Navy Island, by an army raised in the United States, armed in the United States, and at this moment feu from the United States ? CT We learn that an ex pi ess passed through this city for Washington on Monday, with despatches from the British authorities in Canada to the British ministerþÿ filled we doubt not with complaints þÿ and we add without hesitation, well grounded complaints, of the hostile demonstrations of our citizens on the northern frontier. We know that a close correspondence between Mr. Fox and out Government, has been going on for some days. The Express. Canadian Meetings. þÿ A large pubiio meeting on Canada affairs was holden at Middlebury, on the 20lh ult. Gen. T. S« Brown was present and addressed the meeting. The resolutions assumed the right ground, in claiming the right of every American to think, to feel, and to speak, in the cause of liberty, and at the same time declaring that our own laws for the maintenance ef neutrality, must be respected. The. Evening Star. On our frontiers we have repeated public meetings to express sympathy for the Canadians, and this expression of sympathy has been followed by acts violating the laws and existing treaties, as well as the public faith,

which demand the prompt and energetic interference of government, to preserve the whole Union from the probability of a war with England, or at least from estranging the present amicable feelings which are felt and expres-ed by both nations. This is not sympathy þÿ this is war þÿ this is aiding and abetting the citizens of Canada in taking up arms to assail a nation at peace with the United States. Are our people in their senses ? We again say it is the duty of the President to issue his proclamation, and then resort to the ample means he has, to sustain our laws and public treaties. But the fact is, and we say it with deep regret, this is not a movement of Canadians against the colonial government ; it is a movement of Americans against þÿCanada. From the New \ork Morning Herald, Jan. 8. þÿPresident s) Message and Proclamation on t lie affairs of Canada. We publish below the tardy message and proclamation of the President of the United States, on the affairs of Canada. The message, it will be seen, urges the enactment of such measures as will make the neutrality an efficient one, instead of being a mockery and an insult, and is grounded on the letter of the marshal of the northern district of this state, which we also annex. Further particulars will be found in our Washington letter of the 5th instant, in another part of our paper. The þÿPresident proclamation s is as strong as it Can be, and if it only enforced in a bona fide manner, may yet prevent incalculable mischief. By the President of the United States of America. A PROCLAMATION. Whereas, information having been received of a dangerous excitement on the northern irontier of the United States, in consequence of the civil war begun in Canada, and instructions having been given to the United States officers on that frontier, and applications having been made to the Governors of the adjoining States to prevent any unlawful inter ference on the part of our citizens in the contest unfortunately commenced in the British Provinces : additional information has just been received, that, notwithstanding the proclamations of the Governors of the States of New York and Vermont, exhorting the citizens to refrain from any unlawful acts within the territory of the United States; and notwithstanding the presence of the civil officers

of the United States, who, by my directions, have visited the scenes of commotion wi'li the view of impressing the citizens with a proper sense of their duty, the excitement, instead of being appeased is every day increasing in degree þÿ that arms and munitions of war, and other supplies, have been procured by the insurgents in the United States þÿ that a military force, consisting, in part at least, of citizens of the United States, had been actually organized, had congregated at Navy Island, and were still in arms under the command of a citizen of the United States, and that they were constantly receiving accessions and aid. Now, therefore, to the end that the authority of the laws may be maintained, and the faith of treaties observed, I Martin Van Bi ren, do most earnestly exhort all citizens of the United States who have thus violated their duties, to return peaceably to their respective homes; aud 1 hereby warn them, that any persons who shall compromit the neutrality of this Government by interfering in an unlawful manner with the affairs of the neighboring British Provinces, will render themselves liable to arrest and punishment tinder the laws of the United States, which will be rigidly enforced ; and, also, that they will receive no aid or countenance from their government into whatever difficulties they may be thrown by the violation of the laws of their country, and of the territory of a neighboring aud friendly nation. Given under my hand at the city of Wash-
ington, the fifth day of January, A. I). 18.18, and the sixty-second of the independence of the United Slates M. Van Buiien. By (he President : John Forsyth, Secretary of Slate.

From the Barbadian, January 13, 1838. We have commenced in our present impression a report, from the Antigua Weekly Register, of proceedings in the Legislature of that island, which have arisen, out of a very unexpected measure of the Governor-General, Sir William Colebrooke. His Excellency has issued his Proclamation tor the election, j on tiie 1st February, of five members to serve as Representatives from each of the Islands under his command, and summoning them, when so elected, to meet him in a General Council and Assembly at Saint þÿJohn s, Antigua, on the 15th February. It appears by a Circular from Sir William j Colebrooke, of the 21st December, addressed to the Lieutenant-Governors or Presidents of the several Leeward Islands, that no General Assembly of this kind has been convened since the year 1798, at which period the attention of the British parliament was earnestly directed to the condition of the servile classes in the Colonies ; and, that Assembly passed an Act of Amelioration, a Memorial of the humane and liberal spirit during the interval in which the Government J tells Sir William to try if he likes. thing, which characterized its proceedings. That, of the Islands was separately administered, the General Assembly could not be convened ; but, on the re-establishment of the General Government a recurrence to the system was distinctly contemplated. That the near approach of the first period of full emancipation, indicates the importance of making timely provision, in order to secure to the Colonics

the benefits of the sacrifice made for their welfare by the British people. Very good, Sir William þÿ if it had been indeed made exclusively for the benefit of (he Colonists þÿ But, was it ? The carrying out this measure, therefore, successfully, and a revision of the laws which govern the Elective Franchise so as to meet the alterations which a long interval of time has effected in the relative condition of the Colonial Comþÿgress, munities, and the great changes now in pro- will be matters of deliberation in the ! principal buyers ensuing General Assembly The promulgation of the document, (of which we have sketched the substance above) has excited no little ferment in Antigua. The Council and Assembly arc very indignant at this proceeding of the Governor-General.

They were occupied three days consecutively in deliberation on the subject, and (inallv drew up addresses, (both Council and Assemblv) to Sir William Colebrooke, expressing their disapprobation of the measure, and their opinion that it is illegal and inexpedient. The Governor-General returned a courteous answer in explanation of his reasons, which, however, failed to convince the Council and Assembly Their reply to his Excellency breathes a determined spirit of opposition to the measure. The Editor of the Dominica Colonist eontends that Dominica according to an Act of j George 111. in the year 1775, cannot come within the operation of this Proclamation. Such a Convention, if it take place, will be qnite a grand affair in Colonial Legislative History. We wonder if the Govcrnor-Genej ral of these Windward Islands will take the j hint, and bring representatives from St. Vincent, Grenada, and Tobago, to a giand Convention in this island. We confess we aie disposed to think favourably of some measure of this kind. It may be advantageous to the Colonies to discuss in a general Convention the passing of preparatory laws to meet the important coming events, in a friendly and brotherly feeling ; and that all the Islands may have a code of laws as nearly similar as local circumstances will admit for their future government. There may be a very agreeable sort of collision between the talents and experience ol the representatives of the respective islands under one general government, which may elicit some impor-

tant results. The objection, however, þÿ and a very reason;' hie objection it is, þÿ that the men to be sent from the Leeward Islands to Antigua to take part in a general discussion of I aws proper to be enacted, are not gentlemen already forming part of the respective Assemblies, but are to be elected for the specific purpose by (lie freeholders ; and as the qualification is very low, any Tom, Dick, and Harry may be sent from the Towns, and the interests of the great body of the landed proprietors not he represented at all. The scheme seems to have originated entirely with Sir Wm. Colebrooke, who first suggested it to Lord Glenels. The Money Market, London nov. 30. City, Saturday Evening. It is highly satisfactory to be enabled to communicate the fact that a very considerable improvement lias taken place, not only in the demand for the public securities, but in commercial affairs. By letters received from the manufacturing districts to-day we learn that the markets for wollens, cottons, andsilk goods have assumed a stale of great animation, and that as far as the two first articles arc concerned, the principal sales are for the American trade. The actual sales of cotton at Liverpool this week have been nearly 38,300 bales, of which only about 13,000 were on speculation, the spinners having been the for immediate consumption, to supply the demand w hich had commenced on the part of iho manufacturers. Brices of all the stable articles are on the rise, and as the stock of cotton is now reduced to 170,000 bales, or 00,000 bales, less than it was at the same period of last year, it is fully expected that prices will still further advance.

From the St. Thomas Times, Jan. 31 1838. On the 28th instant was celebrated the 70th Anniversary of our beloved Sovereign, King FREDER1K VI. with every demonstration of happy feelings and gratitude to Divine Providence, which had restored His Majesty to the enjoyment of perfect good health, after a dangerous and protracted illness. The day was ushered in by a lloyal Salute of 27 guns from Christiansfort, during which the Musical Band of the Militia performed. At 10 þÿo clock in the forenoon Divine Service was celebrated, on which occasion a detachment of the Garrison was ordered to Church-Parade His þÿMajesty B s rig St. Thomas, laying in the harbour, was tastefully decorated with a number of flags, gave a Royal Salute at noon, and exhibited lire works in the evening. A Levee was held by His Excellency the Governor Chamberlain von Sobotker C. D. and D þÿM at Government House, where the glasses were filled to the health of His Majesty the King under a Royal Salute from Christiansfort. A number of Military, Civil, and Militia Officers as well as of other Inhabitants w'ere invited to a dinner party by His Excellency the Governor, where the healths of Their Majesties were drunk under repeated cheers On account of the generally prevailing sickness the usual Parade of the Garrison and Militia did not take place.

From the St. Christopher Advertiser, Jan. 16. HAYTI. A proclamation has been issued by Boyer, President of Hayti, the contents of which are thus stated by the Philadelphia Inquirer : þÿ Difficulties between France and the Republic of Hayti have arisen, on account of the latter finding it impossible to pay the French indemnity in its full amount. It appears that the president, in a despatch dated 20th May, 1833, offered to reduce the indemnity to seventy-five millions of francs, including the thirty millions forming the loan of Hayti ; and to fix upon a million of francs, annually to be paid till the perfect liquidation of the balance of the account is thus effected. The French minister, far from accepting these propositions, appeared to think, from his reply, dated the 31st July, of the same year, that the wish of the Havtiean Government was to repudiate the old ordinance in order to avoid every engagement ; and he declared that he could recognise no other basis to the question of which he was treating, than the said ordinance. The President says : þÿ In the early part of January of the following year, the French Government sent here as a commissioner, the captain of a ship, Mr. Petit Thouras. He was instructed to demand of the Haytiean Government, the reimburse- | meet the present and prospective changes in ment of the advances which the French trea- j surer had formerly made for the use of the Loan of Hayti ; he was moreover charged to inform himself of the real resources of ihe Republic. The demand for the reimbursement of these

advances was just. It was immediately liquidated by a bill of credit. The French treasure is now returned to their funds. The French government did not recognise these propositions, and a commissioner is now on his way from France, as rumors says, with an armed naval force. On this point the Ilayteati President remarks :

®A»33t þÿTaSTaHB JSlE as'JI&-J3U$-JiTB3 AT'JS. þÿ If the commissioner comes surrounded with the accoutrements of war, w ith the design of imposing upon us conditions which every Iree people should blush to accept, the nation will recall its primitive energy. þÿ It will be faithful to the oath which it has taken, to defend to the last gasp their rights and independence. þÿ Hayteans ; be calm, but be ready for every event."

From the Barbadian, January 13, 1838. At a general Meeting held at the Bible Depository, Mason Hail Street on Thursday the 11th day of January 1838, the following Resolutions were unanimously adopted : Resolved 1st þÿ That the several classes of the populations of this Island being alike subject to the penalties of the laws and the onerous duties of the state, have an equal claim to the protection of those laws in their persons and properties and to all the privileges and advantages of the state. And that the principle oi self government by representation being admitted and carried into practice, they must, therefore, be considered to have an equal claim to a voice in the choice of representatives, until the contrary shall have been clearly established on reasonablegrounds. Resolved 2nd. þÿ That in the present very restricted exercise of the elective franchise by a very small pioportion of the male population ot the island, the great body of the people and tiie immense majority who have a prospective view of the right of election, possess in fact no voice in the Legislature, and therefore have no proper security against the enactment of laws exclusively inimical to their interests. Resolved 3rd. þÿ That from the state of opi nion among the wealthier classes of this Island, and as the laws must now at least in appearance, operate equally on all, it is not at all impossible, that in the present restricted exercise of the franchise, the poor and middle class of every complexion may be called upon to submit to Laws which are only adapted to

a state of Slavery. Resolved 4th. þÿ That the proper remedy for this state of things, and security against this possible abuse of legislative power, can only be lound in the extension of the franchise, to embrace such a proportion of the poor and the middle classes of every complexion as will take from the representatives every inducement to conciliate any one class at the expense the others. of Resolved 5th. þÿ That a committee be appointed prepare Petitions to be presented to to the three branches of Colonial Legislature, praying for a revision of the Election Laws of the Island, and such an extension of the franchise as will embrace an equitable pioportion the poor and middle classes and of

their social relations. Resolved 6th. þÿ That the Petitions when prepared, shall be left open for signaures at such places and during such time as the Committee shall think proper, and of which due notice shall be given in the public Journals. Resolved 7th þÿ I hat these resolutions be published in all the Newspapers. A. Fim.an, Chairman. S. J. Prescod, Secretary.

St. Croix, CHRIS TIAN ST ED, ( THURSDA Y) February 8, 1838. Both the second December and first January mails from England arrived here after our last Gazette was printed. The Canadas are the engrossing subject in England, þÿ the Atlas of the 31st December states that it was decided, alter a consultation between Lord Glenelg and Lord Hill, Commander in chief, that 5,000 additional troops should be embarked for Canada as early in the spring as the navigation would permit their reaching Quebec. Lord J. Russell declared the determination of Government to protect and support the Loyal British subjects of Canada. Messrs. þÿO Connell, Hume and Leader affirm that there are only two proper courses to be adopted by the ministry either to grant the disaffected Canadians the changes they have asked in their colonial government, or to give them their Independence. Parliament had adjourned over the holy days, from December 23rd to January 16th, and Lord John Russell had given notice that on the last named day the affairs of Canada would be brought before Parliament The new Erench Chambers were opened by H. M Louis Phillippe in person, H. R H. the Duke De Nemours was present having just arrived from Africa; he had fractured his arm in an accidental fall on board ship. Mr. Dupin was elected President of the Chamber of Deputies >v a considerable majority. Marshal Vullee is named commander in chief of the French þÿposses- >ns in Africa. A new attempt against the life of the King had been discovered and Irustiated by the vigilance of the police. In Spain there bad

been a new change of ministry. Cordova and several of his party, recall'd from France, are reinstated. Espartero was resting on his arms at Painpeluna ; and Don Carlos in Navarre was preparing for a new erruption into the southern provinces. It appears that Lord Gossford & Sir Francis Head retire, at their own request, from the Government of the Canadas. General Sir John Colbourne is to have the Government of Lower Canada, and Col. Sir George Arthur is appointed Lieutenant Governor of the upper province þÿ the latter has been breveted Major General

Substitute for Indigo. þÿ Public attention has been latterly attracted in France by the reported perfection to which the discovery of a substitute for indigo has been brought, and by the establishment of dye works on a large

soale for applying the process to the dying ol wool and woollen cloths, for which it is more especially suited It appears that so far hack as the public exposition of the products of art and industry for 131, two pieces of kerseymore were exhibited amongst the assortment of cloths from the manufactory of M. (-unin Gridaine, one of the largest and most reputed amongst the French woollen manufacturers, which were dyed upon the new principle. þÿ The cloths were purposely selected, it is said, of a strong iriake and extremely close texture, so as to test the virtue of the dying matter more completely. The result is stated, according to the renort of the jury or council, to have been entirely successful, a beautiful even c >! > t ins? t- winced the one piece þÿ being of a i: and the other of a deep biue, of superb mat re This new product is called French bine (/>.«.-; Jn France), and its advantages arc tints scribed : 1st. Its colour, in þÿ all its shades, is of very superior beauty to anything yet known. 2d. It is perfectly unchangeable by air, acids, soaps, &c. 3d. It never whitens at the seams, like indigo. 4th. It dyes in or penetrates the piece in the most perfect manner, which cannot be done with indigo. 5th It preserves the quality of the cloth with all its softness and suppleness, without in any way altering the texture or nap. 6th.
