The Commercial Journal of Guadeloupe quotes a letter from Martinique, informing of the arrival there on the 1 1 th ult. of the French Frigate, Iphigenie, which is to be placed at the disposal of Rear Admiral De Bretonnierke, the officer appointed by the French Government to command the intended expedition to St. Domingo. And, in the Martinique Courier, we find that the Squadron will, besides the Iphigenie consist of La Didon, La Nercide, La Bergerc, Le Nisus, L'Oreste, La Griffon, and probably, La Therpsichore. M. De Bretonnierre had arrived at Brest to assume the command of this squadron, which will convey troops to St. Domingo; the object being, as we have lately remarked, to force the Government of Hayti into the payment of certain claims of the former Mother Country, established by treaty. We have lately published an extract, in which President Boyer declares that if. these French negotiators approach with arms, and with threats, that the Republic will be prepared to resist them. We may expect soon to hear of a dust between the republicans and the forces of the French Monarch. The Baron De Mackau (Govnr. of Martinique) has delayed his departure for France a little longer, on account of some legislative matters, important to the colony, which he wishes to see completed before he retires from the Government. Rear Admiral Duvai, Daii.i.y has been appointed his successor þÿ La A'aide Frigate has sailed from Martinique in pursuit of a Pirate which had chased the

merchant Ship Belisaire into St. Pierre. The attention of the commercial men is beginning to be sensibly alive to the proceedings ot the French government relative to their claim upon St. Domingo. A squadron of 12 ships ot war, it will be recollected, sailed from Brest on the 29th ult, bound to the West Indies, and it is well understood by the mercantile world that the destination is llayti. A commissioner had preceded this expedition, and M. Las Cazes accompanied the fleet as the diplomatic agent of France to the Havtian government, the declared or presumed object being the settlement of the claim of trance, arising out of the Haytian loan, on that state. Such a demonstration of power to back a mere financial arrangement seems so much more than needful, that the mercantile interests of this country connected with Hayti feel great anxiety to ascertain whether the British government are privy to the object of the French government, and how far British property in St. Domingo is safe; and whether they can with prudence make further shipments to that market, or engage shipping to bring home what properly is already there ; because, from the peculiar nature of the trade with St. Domingo, all the shipping engagements must be made in this county. þÿ London Times,

The essence of liberty consists in die freedom ot discussion " '1 hose who in quarrels interpose, " Must often wipe a bloody nose." A few facts for thinking and calculating Americans. The King of France interfered in the American revolution, not from his love of liberty, but his hatred to England. Result. Fie revolutionized his own dominions, and lost his crown and head. Austria and J'russia interfered in the French Revolution. Result. Vienna and Berlin, their capitals, were entered by victorious French armies Napoleon interfered with Russia and marched a victorious army ol half a million of men to Moscow. Result, l'aris captured twice by invading armies. Napoleon bent all bis powers and all his energies to the subjugation of England. Result. 1J e died a prisoner to England on the rock of St. Helena. So much for the past. Prophecy ! þÿ Americans will interfere in the revolt in Canada. Results. A declaration of war against America by England ; an alliance offensive and defensive between England and Mexico; the ocean swarming with British and Mexican piivatecrs; British steam irigates and privateers on all the great lakes, where they have little to lose and much to gain ; the ports of Mexico defended by British fleets and garrisons ; an Anglo Mexican fleet and army hovering on the South ; an.expedition fitted out in the West Indies with an army of free blacks, to sympathize and take part with two millions of slaves in the Southern States, and co-operate with the abolition-

ists of the North ; the Indians in the West, removed from their native soil by force, raising the tomahawk and scalping knife, and carrying fire and slaughter into the Western states on a frontier of a thousand miles, and finally a Dissolution of the I nion. So much for interference in the quarrels of others, even if on understanding the question thoroughly, you take the right side If you set your neighbors house on fire, a change of wind may bring the flames you have kindled to your own dwellings. England, peace at with all the world, cannot, and will not, be treated in Canada as Mexico was in Texas A treaty between nations is virtually a contract between all the individuals of each nation. Americans be honest, and fulfil your contracts in the face of the whole world ! þÿ You cannot honestly assist the enemies ot England, even by words. A Friend of Feace and Good Will.

As soon as the journal was read, a Message from the President of the United States, by his Private Secretary, was announced ; and which, on motion, was immediately read, as follows : To the Senate, and Hons" of Representatives of the. United States : In the highly excited state of feeling on the Northern frontier, occasioned hy the disturbances in Canada, it was to be apprehended that causes of complaint might arise on the lino dividing the United Stales front her Britannic Majesty's dominions. Every precaution was therefore taken on our part, authorized by the existing laws ; and as the troops of the provinces were embodied on the Canadian side, it was hoped that no serious violation of the rights of the United States would be permitted to occur. I regret however, to inform you that an outrage of a most aggravated character has been committed, accompanied by a hostile though temporary invasion of our territory, producing the strongest feelings of resentment on the part of our citizens in the neighborhood, and on the whole border line ; and that the excitement previously existing has been ularmingly increased. To guard against the possible recurrence of any similar net, 1 have thought it indispensable to call out a portion of the militia, to be posted on that, frontier. The documents herewith presented to Congress, show the character of the outrage committed, the measures taken in conse-

quence of its occurrence, and the necessity for resorting to them. It will also he seen that the subject was immediately brought to the notice of the British Minister accredited to this country, and the proper steps taken on our part to obtain the fullest infoimation of all the circumstances leading to and attendant upon the transaction, preparatory to a demand for reparation. 1 ask such appropriations as the circumstances in which our country is thus unexpectedly placed require. M. VAN buren.

RECOVERY FROM HYDROPHOBIA. (From the Cry Ion Colette, June 17, 1812.) If the alleviation or cure of the most formidable disease to which mankind is incident be a source of satisfactory reflection to society, the case which we are here to submit to our readers may well warrant our congratulations. as, from the period of the introduction of vaccination by Dr Jenner to the present time, a discovery of such value and importance has not been made in the practice of medicine as that which is the subject of our present remarks. We shall now proceed to state the outlines of the case, promising only that it was treated by Dr. Shoolbred, surgeon of the native Hospital, who has had the good fortune to be the first, to introduce to Bengal this successful method of treating hydrophobia. On Tuesday, the 5th curt,, a Bheestee, who had been bitten 3 weeks before in the leg by a mad dog, was carried to the Native Hospital, about 3 o'clock in the alternoon, with the symptoms of hydrophobia strongly upon him. He was immediately bled to the extent of 10 ounces. þÿ The symptoms cf the disease yielded in succession as the blood flowed ; and before the vein was closed, he stretched out bis hand for a cup of water, and calmly drank it off, though the mere approach of the water but a few minutes before had thrown him into convulsions. After the bleeding, he laid down on a cot, fell asleep, and continued so for nearly two hours. þÿ When he awoke the symptoms of the disease were threatening to return ; another vain was then opened, and 8 ounces

more of blood were taken away, which so completely subdued the disease, that he has not had a symptom of it since. We are anxious to lose no time in making this important fact known to the public, as at this season particularly its immediate publication may be the means of saving the lives of some individuals. The Bheestee, who is the subject of the foregoing case, being still in the hospital, we need say no more at this time ; but in our next number we hope to present our readers with a detail of this most satisfactory, and we may add, unprecedented case in the annals of medicine. We may, howexer, further add, that the earlier the practice is adopted after the appearance of unequivocal symptoms of hydrophobia, the greater is the chance of success ; and thiit therefore persons whose servants may be attacked with this formidable disease should not allow them to waste time in incantations and other useless practices commonly resorted to by the natives on such occasions, but cause them to be placed as quickly as possible under the charge of a regular practitioner. In conclusion, we must add, that the benefit of this discovery is probably not confined to cases of hydrophobia, for as the cure of this disease has apparently been missed for 2000 years, by considering it as a disease of the nervous class, and as particularly analagous to tetanus, wo are thence, perhaps, justified in the hope that the latter, which is scarcely less fatal than by hydrophobia, may be cured by pursuing the unalogy in an opposite direc-
tion, and applying to tetanus, and perhaps other affections, the treatment which has just been proved to be so successful in hydrophobia. Water-carrier.

The humble Petition of the Undersigned Agriculturists ot the said Island sheweth, That your Petitioners beg leave to approach your Excellency with the heartfelt expression of their feelings of loyalty and duty to the Grown. T hat your Petitioners are persons engaged in Agriculture, and drawing their whole subsistence from the soil. That this Island is essentially an agricultural community, the prosperity of everv other class, being altogether dependent on the well being of the Planters, add that a revenue of wore than £300 000 is annually derived from this Island to the Crown. That notwithstanding the productiveness of the soil, and the great value of its exports, this Island as absolutely incapable of furnishing a sufficient supply of the common necessaries of life, for the support of its agricultural population, and that in seasons of scarcity and distress to which it is peculiarly exposed, your Petitioners in common with the great mass ot Agricultural Labourers are reduced to a dependence on the resources of the Proprietary Body. That the right of the Proprietors in the election of Representatives for the Assembly is at present reduced below its just standard by the absence of the major part of them in England, and that the convocation of a «eneral Council and Assembly will by minding

the Constituencies of the towns and divisions together, absolutely annihilate the small re mains of that just and constitutional influence which they have hitherto been permitted to enjoy.' That your Petitioners consequently view with feelings of alarm, and dismay, the measures which are now in operation for transferring the Legislation of this Colony, not merely into the hands of those who have no direct interest in the cultivation of the soil, but absolutely into those of the three smallest and least important of the neighbouring Colonies. That your Petitioners further beg leave respectfully to submit to your Excellency that any attempt to re-establish the Legislature of the Leeward Carribbee Islands, which, " shortly after the close of the late war were dissolved into separate Governments" will be unconstitutional and derogatory of the Royal Authority. That your Petitioners therefore humbly pray your Excellency to reconsider the subject and to adopt such measures as to your Excellency's wisdom may seem fit to stay proceedings which your Petitioners cannot but view as alike opposed to the interests of the subject and to the authority and dignity of the Crown. All the commercial advices from the United States concur in stating that the prevailing opinion there is that, notwithstanding the elections had gone strongly against the Van Burcn party, the President would persevere

in his currency projects so long as he held the executive ; the tone of his message indicated that he would do so. In consequence there is an impression amongst well informed parties in the United States that it is doubtful whether many of the banks are inclined to resume specie payments, and of many who have the inclination the ability is questioned This view of the state of many of the banks in the United States is considered to be an impartial one, approximating nearer to the truth than the contents of many of the letters of a few weeks past. Indeed, the want of a second medium of currency was confirmed by the determination of the executive of the United States to issue treasury notes. But there is one fact which has excited the attention of our monetary men, and is also an object of interest to our commercial men, whose prosperity depends upon a steady paper currency, founded upon a sound metallic basis : it is, that within the short period between 1833 and 1830 the paper money in the United States had increased from 80,000,000 to 120,000,000 of dollars, and the metal money from 29,0000,000 to 73,000,000 of dollars, being an increase in the amount of specie in the United States of 44,000.000 of dollars, or ten millions sterling in that short time ; or rather, let us remind our readers an increase of 150 per cent ; of which vast augmentation the greater portion yet remains in the United States. Our men of business will appreciate this curious illustration, which shows that one

country alone, in a very short space of time, has been able to .bsorb £10,000,000 sterling of bullion frern the common stock of the world; that, too, during a period when luxury was tempting an increase in the manufacture of gold and silver articles, whilst the increase from tne mines was comparatively trifling. But it shows that our monetary system, as at present conducted at the Bank of England, under their charter, is far from being secure; it shows the folly of the Bank corporation attempting any foreign agency to employ their bullion (which we have denied), and its extreme danger ; in lact there is no great cause of exultation on the part of the Bank ; for the present large amount of bullion in their coffers, unless they use it to some better purpose, may be drawn away sooner than many anticipate, if the measures of Mr. Van Buren compel the banks in the United States to resume specie payments, in order to sustain their credit against a government paper, which is forced amongst the people to absorb the specie, to suit the views and for the use of the executive. These circumstances, in the aggregate, deserve the most serious consideration of our own government, and point at the immediate necessity of reforming the Bank of England charter, so that that institution may either become less the slave of the government and more useful to the community, or that its functions should be limited alone to government services. þÿ London payer.

THE LATE ROYAL EXCHANGE. This fine edifice was the earliest and most interesting memorial of England's commercial prosperity, which was followed, as a natural consequence, by a degree of maratime power and colonial extensions unknown to any other nation in any age of the world. þÿ With a degree of sagacity equal to anv we meet with in the records of history, Elizabeth saw that commerce was to be the great machine by which the native energies of the people were to be developed, and the country brought to a high state of wealth and civilization. And well was this trulv great and British Queen seconed by the masculine wisdom of the truly British statesmen whom the superior discernment of her mind had selected to promote the prosperity, the honour, independence, and glory of Great Bi itain. It is impossible for patriotic feeling to witness the awtul destruction of so noble a monument of British commerce, without sentiments of deep regret, and such honourable feeling, we are gratified to find, is more extensive than our modern cosmopolites could imagine, and which they are incapable ol appreciating. This national building, we need hardly say, was presented to the nation by Sir Thomas Gresham, a merchant. It was first opened as a Royal Exchange in November 1 587 ; consequently in the earlier part of Queen Elizabeth's reign, and was then styled the Bourse ; but three years after (Jan. 23, 1570), on the visit of the Queen and her court to the city, when her Majesty dined with Sir Thomas Gresham, at his mansion in Bishops-

gate-slreet, this illustrious Sovereign caused her herald to proclaim by sound of trumpet, tint henceforth it should be called the Royai Exchange. At his decease Sir Thomas Gresham bequeathed it to his widow, with remainder to the mayor and citizens of London, and ;o the Mercer's Company, directing that the rents should be chiefly devoted to the support of lectures on arts and sciences. In 1 060 the original edifice was destroved by the great fire, and it was Sir Christopher W ren who had the honour of rebuilding it as it recently stood, and nearly upon its original plan, except the tower, which was said to he designed by Hawksmoor. However, the new building was rapidly advanced and completed with the statues of the Kings and Queens, and Sir T. Grcsham, as they were originally placed. It was completed lor less than 80,000/. It was opened to the public on the 28th of September, 1069, that is, about three jears after the destruction of its predecessor.
A person named Jerman was then cit surveyor, and was employed to superintcn the work.

On the day appointed for this opening, a committee of the first class citizens and merchants assembled to meet King Charles II., whom they had reason to expect would have performed that ceremony in person ; but his .Majesty did not gratify the citizens, wherefore the then lord mayor, Sir Wm. Turner, took it upon him, and perambulated the arcades twice in procession with the aldermen, other city authorities, and the committee, and his lordship made an address to the assembled merchants, congratulating them on the restoration to them of so noble and useful a building Some ten or eleven years ago it was thoroughly and substantially repaired, and the clock tower reconstructed from designs made bv Mr. Geo. Smith architect to the Mercer's Company, and the expense was defrayed by the said company and the corporation of London. Amongst the present Gresharn Committee are the lord mayor, Aldermen Thompson, Farebrother, and Winchester, and eight members of the common council, with an equal number of the Mercer's Company. The lectures, which is probable may be suspended this term, are divinity, civil law, music, astronomy, rhetoric, geometry, and physic, of which there are four courses given every year ; that is, one course in each of the law terms. It is said that the different rebuildings and repairs have cost the corporation and the mercer's company above 200,000/. þÿ Morning Herald , Jan. 12.

( From the Boston Daily Advertiser, Feb. 8.) Death of O scola. We learn from our correspondents of the Charleston Courier and Southern Patriot, that the celebrated Indian Chief Oscola, died on the night of the 30th ult. at Fort Moultrie, on Sullivan's Island. þÿ 11c died of a disease of the throat, by which he had been confined to his bed lor some days previous Death of Oscola. þÿ This far famed Chief paid the debt of nature at Sullivan's Island on Tuesday night He had been sick for some time þÿ when we saw him at the Theatre, he looked sad and tired of the world He was attacked wiih a catarrhal fever, but whether he fell a victim to the common course of the disease, or to the harrassmenU of a vexed and disappointed spirit, is a matter of doubt þÿ probably a combination of the two. He bad tiie best medical attendance and we believe was in nothing neglected þÿ but it would not do- -his proud and unconquerable spirit refused to be chained to a captive body. We shall not write his epitaph or Ins funeral oration, yet there is something in the character of this man not unworthy of the respect of the world. From a vagabond child, he became the master spirit of a long and desperate war. He made himself þÿ no man owed less to accident. Bold and decisive in action, deadly but consistent in hatred, dark in revenge, cool, subtle, sagacious in council, he established gradually and surely a resistless ascendancy over his adopted tribe, by the d.nirig ol his deeds, the constancy of bis hostility to the whites, and the profound cralt of

Ins policy. In council he spoke þÿlittle he made the other chiefs his instruments, and what they delivered in public, was the secret suggestion of the invisible master. Such was Oscola, who will be long remembered as the man that with the feeblest means produced the most terrible effects þÿ Charleston Mercury.

This morning, shortly before five o'clock, the cry of fire resounded through the streets, und the illuminating glare which immediately succeeded, and spread over the city, even to its western limits, gave fearful signs of the reality and extent of the conflagration. It was soon known that the cause of alarm proceeded from the Theatre and Circus, on Front street, Old Town. Owing to the extreme cold, which compelled a more than usual still- Dess and quiet during the waning hours of night, the tire, which appears to have broken out near the centre of the building, was not discovered until it had gained great headway. When the alarm was first given, nearly the whole interior was enveloped in flames ; and on bursting open the door of the stables attached thereto, in which were kept the numerous and valuable stud of horses belonging to Mr (moke, the Manager, the instant rushing out of the flames prevented all possible ingress, as it also too plainly showed that all ingress had already become useless. All efforts, and these were constant and oft repeated, to save the house, or any part of its contents, proved vain and ineffectual The destructive element held on its fierce course, and in a couple of hours, this spacious and costly edifice was a heap of ruins. Nothing remains of it now, but a portion of its bare and blackened walls At an early period after the alarm was first given, the fire exten ded across the narrow street which bounds the Circus on the South, and reached the large

brick building on the opposite corner, occupied as a tavern by Mr. P. Murphy. Great efforts were made by the fire department to save this property, but they were equally unsuccessful, and the whole establishment, front and rear, extending from Front street to the Falls, is also destroyed, save the bare walls. Mr. Murphy's loss in furniture and other valuables is heavy, the greater portion of the contents of the house being destroyed with it. But the heaviest individual sufferer is Mr. Cooke, the enterprising manager ol the Circus. His whole wardrobe and other stage property, and nearly the whole of his equestrian establishment, among the most valuable in the country, was involved in destruction with the building. Of fifty two horses, connected with this establishment, it is said that only five were rescued ; the others, it is supposed, were suffocated by the smoke and flame before they had time to raise their appalling cry of alarm. As to the origin of the fire, it can only be a subject of conjecture. There was an equestrian performance in the Circus the previous evening, which was concluded with the dramatic representation of Mazeppa, and the Wild Horse, and it is not unlikely that the catastrophe was the accidental result of the large fires, which the extreme cold of the evening rendered necessary. The numerous lights which are required in all parts of the house, on the evenings of performance, may also have had some accidental agency in

From the Barbadian, February 10 LOWER CANADA. We conceive all information on the subject of this province to have been made interesting bv recent events, and subjoin therefore some Extracts from the work of that intelligent traveller the author of Cyril Thornton. "On the day following, 1 drove to Montreal ; and was certainly agreeably surprised by the appearance of the City. It stands on an Island, about 30 miles long and at a short distance from the mountain whose name it bears The houses are entirely constructed of stone ; and the neatness of the buildings, and the general air of solidity and compactness, have a very pleasing effect to an eve accustomed to the trashy clap board edifices of an American town. It is the fashion at Montreal to cover the roofs of the houses with tin, so that in looking down on it from the neighbouring heights, the city glitters with a mirror-like brightness. In the higher part of the town are some handsome streets, and the public buildings are in the best taste þÿ plain, substantial, and without pretension any sort. of The population of Montreal is about 3d, 000. The great majority of the mercantile class are English, But the lower orders, both in language and appearance, decidedly French. Their dress is at once primitive and peculiar. Like the Spaniards, they wear a sort of coloured worsted round the waist, a jacket, generally of blue or brown, and shoes fashioned after the Indian Mocassin. The natives of the Montreal and Quebec districts are distinguished by the color of their caps. The

former wear the bonnet blue, and the latter bonnet rouge. The prevailing religion is the Catholic, and the cathedral does honor to the taste and spirit of the inhabitants. 1 passed a week at Montreal, with great pleasure, and then embarked in one of those magnificent steamers which plv on the St. Lawrence for Quebec. The distance between the cities is one hundred and eighty miles, which is generally accomplished in about 20 hours. As we approached Quebec, the scenery became more wild and mountainous. Cultivation rarely extends beyond a mile or two from the river, and agriculture appears to be conducted by the Canadians of the lower province on the worst principles To me, they appeared a light-hearted and amiable people, who brave the chances of life, with apathy to its suflcnniTs, and a keen sensation of its enjoyments. No contrast in human character can be greater than that exhibited by the inhabitants of Lower Canada and the United States. The one, averse from all innovation, content to live as his fathers have done before him, sluggish, inert, and animated by strong local attachment to the spot of his activity. The other, active and speculating, never satisfied with his present condition, emigrating wherever interest may direct, and influenced in every circumstance by the great principle "I turning the penny. The Canadian is undoubtedly the more interesting; but on the standard of utility, 1 fear Jean Baptiste must yield the pox to Jonathan. Quebec bears on its front the impress of

nobility. By the most obtuse traveller, it connol be mistaken for a mere common place and vulgar city. It towers with an air of pride and of menace þÿ the menace not of a bully, but of an armed Faladin prepared for

battle. No city in the world stands amid nobler scenery. The heights bristling with works ; the splendid and impregnable citadel frowning on Cape Diamond ; the river emerging in the distance from the dark pine forest, with its broad expanse covered with ship- j ping ; the Isle of Orleans reposing in tranquil beauty amid its waters ; and the colossal ranges of mountains which close the prospect, þÿ constitute an assemblage of splendid features which may be equalled but can scarcely be surpassed. Close to the city are the Plains of Abraham, Traces of field works are yet visible, and an oval block of granite marks the spot on which Wolfe expired ; about a mile higher is Wolfe's Cove, where be landed during the night, and the fearful cliffs up which he led his followers to victory. A redoubt on the summit was carried by an escalade, and by day-dawn the army was formed in order of battle on the heights. Montcalm instantly quitted his entrenchments at Beaufort, to meet him. By ten o'clock the armies were engaged, and in two hours the power of France, on the American continent, was annihilated. The Citadel has been strengthened and rebuilt at an enormous expense. It perfectly commands both the city and the river, and is so strong, that in all human probability it will ever remain a virgin fortress. At all events, those who have skill, courage, and energy to wrest it from the grasp of British soldiers, will deserve to keep it. Assuredly their national annals will record no more

brilliant achievement. The village of Loretto is a melancholy sight. þÿ It contains the last and only remains of the once powerful tribe of Huron Indians. Brandy and gunpowder have done their work, and about two hundred of this once noble people, are all that survive. They have adopted the religion and speak die language of tiie Canadians. There is a Church in the village, and a priest who mingles with his flock, and is beloved by them. Christianity is the only benefit for which the red man is indebted to the white. þÿ The latter cheats, robs, corrupts, and ruins him in this world, and then makes a merit of saving him in the next. The benefit is pure, but these poor Indians may reasonably distrust the gift, where there is blood on the hand by which it is bestowed. Mr. Papincau and his party arc continually grumbling at being subject to British dominion ; but what would they have ! They pay no taxes. John Bull spends his money pretty freely among them, as they may see bv the works on Cape Diamond, and the Kideau canal. The latter must be of immediate and great benefit to both provinces, but had the Canadians been left to their own resources, it could never have existed. What would they have ? The lower province at least will not join the United States ; audit is too poor, and too helpless, to set up for itself. Withdraw British Capital from the Colony, and what would remain ? Rags, poverty, and empty harbours. When Lower Canada first canie into the possession of Great Britain, the latter com-

mitted a great error in not insisting that her language should be adopted in all public instruments. The consequence is, that eighty years have passed, and the people are still French. The tie of community of literature does not exist, and the only channel by which moral influence can be asserted or maintained.

has been wantonly closed. The people read þÿ when they read any thing þÿ French books; French authorities are quoted in the Law Courts, the French language is spoken in the streets ; French habits ; French feelings, French prejudices, abound every where. The lapse of three generations has witnessed no advancement, moral or intellectual, in the Canadians of the Lower Province. They are now precisely what they were at the period of the conquest. Another decided blunder was the separation of Canada into two provinces. This has prevented any general amalgamation of it e population One province is decidedly I'rench; the other no less exclusively Lnglish, or American. The latter enjoys a milder climate, and more fertile soil, and increases in wealth and population far more rapidly than its rival. It is to the upper province that the whole tide of emigration is directed. It is with produce of the Upper province that the ships navigating the St. Lawrence are freighted ; Lower Canada exports little but lumber. The French Canadians, therefore oppose every improvement by which the rival province may be benefitted, and, with such feelings, collision on a thousand points is unavoidable. Internal improvement is impeded, for there could be no agreement as to the proportion of contribution to be furnished by each province. The breach, instead of healing, is annually widening and Upper Canada is thrown into an intercourse with the United States the result of which 1 have already ven-

tured to predict. The government of Canada may in one sense be called a bed of roses, for it is full of thorns. Every governor must find it so. þÿ He has to deal with men of mean minds and selfish passions ; to maintain the necessary privileges of the Crown ; to prevent the rational freedom of a limited monarchy from degenerating into the unbridled license of democracy. He is beset by clamour, and assailed by faction, and must either become the leader of one party, or offend both. His difficulties and embarrassments increase. He appeals for support to his government, and receives a letter of thanks and his recall, The travels of the Schoolmaster have not yet led him lo these wintry regions. Few of the lower order of Canadians can read, and the education even of the more wealthy is defective, The ladies resemble those of the United States, and are subject to the same prematurity of decay. But they are pleasing and amiable, though given to commit sad slaughter among sensitive and romantic subalterns. The old stagers are generally charm proof, and the marriage of a major is an event as remarkable in the colony as the appearance of a comet. þÿ Jamaica Fotypheme, January 6«

This seems to have been written in the spirit of prophecy, þÿ and it has been fulfilled in the flattering letters of approbation from Lord Glenelg to Sir F. B. Head, and bis recall after having achieved -wonders as a Civil Governor. þÿ Edit. Barb.

The Packet Ships þÿ The ships England, Garrick, and Philadelphia, having sailed this morning, there are now only two packet ships in port, the Erie, to sail to-morrow, for Havre, and the Pennsylvania, for Liverpool on the 8th, should all the packets have sailed on their regular days, from the European ports, there are now twenty-seven on their way to this port. By the following paragraph, from the Baltimore Sun it appears that the Cooke family, which lately suffered so severe a loss by the destruction of their stud cf horses, have again been burned out. þÿ A variety of distressing incidents of a domestic nature resulted from the fire, which were peculiarly felt by the family of the Cookes, who boarded in the house. The lady of one of the sons, confined some time during the past week, was hastily snatched from her bed, and hurried to an adjourning street, under the agonizing belief that her babe bad perished ; it was, however, removed by some of the firemen in safety. The northern mail of this morning has brought us advices from the frontier. We believe that every arsenal on the New York border has been broken open and robbed by ! the band of lawless þÿ þÿpirates infesting the frontier, and claiming to be þÿ patriots! Tru j espouse. ly, if they are patriots, then was þÿJohnson s sarcastic difmition true, that þÿ Patriotism is the last refuge of a þÿscoundrel. It will be seen that the Governor has issued a proclamation for the purpose of recovering the public property, and has called upon the legislature for assistance. The officers of þÿ the þÿparty along the lines, it seems, cannot be entrusted with the execution of the laws, and a batch of special attornies are wanted, to be taken from Suffolk county, or somowhercelse, where the fire of patriotism burns less fiercely.

The following is from a Canada paper þÿ the Sandwich Herald, of Feb. 17. Part of it we know to be untrue, but there is probably some truth in the remainder. The cannon, for instance, which has all been recovered þÿ and the alleged presence of Van Rensselaer, who lias riot been near Detroit. An attack is contemplated by the pirates upon that part of the province nearly, if not immediately; opposite the village of Palmer, on the river St. Clair. One circumstance goes far in corroboration of this fact, which

®AWSK TSStrcTOJMSJK ®2©a'JS®IIWt>3 AT23. is, that an unusual number of sleighs were seen to pass through the city of Detroit at 12 þÿo clock at night, on Wednesday last, without bells to the horses which drew them. þÿ There is no doubt but they contained pirates, who were going in the direction of St Clair. The following is their mode of travelling þÿ Van Rensselaer and another person go in advance to reconnoitre, in the guise of Yankee pedlars. Their pedlar wagons contain cannon which were obtained by means of a forged order at Buffalo ; on the top are the wares usually hawked about by the Yankee itinerants. The other perons travel in small gangs chiefly it is believed, through Monroe and Ypsilauti, ana so on to the point above stated. In addition to the above named cannon, secreted m the waggons, tlie pirates obtained from the Dearborn arsenal twenty-four cases of firearms. These arms were (ostensibly) destined lor Detroit, and were left unguarded, on the side of the rail road. 1 he pirates immediately possessed themselves of them, and, as usual, a ternbie hue and cry was made about the theft. A Pketty Quarrel. þÿ We have already published þÿPresident Mackenzies letter, impugning the honor of Generalissimo Van Rensselaer. The generalissimo retorts as follows, in a letter to the Albany Daily Advertiser. He has at last arrived at the true character of Ins þÿ þÿGovernment. Messrs. Editors. þÿ It was my intention to have prepared a statement in lull, tor your next paper, ot the late transactions ol the pa-

triot army of Upper Canada, but lind it will take more time than 1 anticipated, and that I cannot get it ready in season. As such a statement has become absolute necessary, however, in order to protect my good name from the malign aspersions of Wm. Lyon Mackenzie , 1 trust you will alibi'd me the space in your columns, now to ask my fellow countrymen to suspend their opinion ol me for a short period. In that case, 1 pledge myself to bring forward facts enough to prove the sudden abandonment of the late expedition in the North, to be chargeable to none but to the said IV. L. Mackenzie. He must stand forth in the true, but unenviable light, of a cruel, reckless, selfish madman, ana as the greatest curse of the cause lie prelends to j

It is true, as he states through the Water- I town Jeffersonian, that 1 have again thrown up my commission of commander-in-chief. þÿ My determination this time, is to assist no farther in the cause, so long as he is in any way connected with it ; and my parting advice to those from either side of the boundary line, who have labored with me so long, and so faithfully, is, turn the meddling craven out of your ranks, þÿ until that is done, you need not even hope for success. þÿREASJ R.VAN RENSSELAER. late commander &.c iVc. BANK MEETING. At a meeting of the banks of the city of New Fork, held on the 2Sth of February, 1838, i the committee on þÿ the resumption of specie payments" submitted the following report , in part, viz : In contemplation of the resumption of specie payments, by the banks of the city of New York, on or before the 10th of May next, and under the uncertain contingency of a simultaneous or early resumption by the banks of some of the other great commercial cities, it is incumbent on those of New York j to adopt all the measures within the limits of their resources, which may enable them not only to resume, but also to maintain specie payments. Much has already been done in that respect. the result, as well of causes not r rider the control of the banks, as of positive action on their part. 1. It appears by the annual returns of the bank commissioners, that, exclusively of the Dry Dock Bank, which is not included in the return of this year, the gross amount of all the liabilities of the city banks, payable on demand deducting therefrom the notes and checks of other banks held by them, and the balances due to them by other banks, amounted, on the 1st of January 1836, to 820.918,105 ; on the 1st January, 1837, to 825,185,287 ; and on the 1st January 1N38, 812,920,601 þÿ making a diminution in the liabilities of more than twelve millions and a half during the year 1837. 2. The detailed statement for the 1st Jan. 1838, rendered l>v the several city banks to their standing committee, shows a balance to

their credit of more than four millions due to them by the banks out ot the state, and of j more than two millions in account with all j the banks out of the city. Ample means, as also appears by those statements, have been provided bv the country banks of the state, for the redemption of their notes, which circulate in the city On a view of the whole subject, vve may confidently sav, that the relative strength of the bunks is, and at the time of the resumption will be, greater than it was during the last two years, and probably at any former time. The fall in the rate of foreign exchanges, now considerably below par in our city paper, renders it absolutely certain, that no exportation specie can take place, and more of than probable that a considerable influx may be expected. This fact, now indisputable, must have an effect on public opinion, and ought to remove the apprehensions of those who may have believed our efforts for an early resumption premature. Secure, as all the banks in the United States are, against foreign demands, we arc justified in expecting their co operation. If this is obtained, we do not perceive any obstacle to an early, easy, and sale resumption of specie payments. A continued suspension, on the part of some of the other great commercial cities, can alone render the resumption on our part difficult, and may prevent a free application

of the legitimate resources of Now York. þÿ Yet. such is the favorable relative siate of the balances between this and the other parts of the union, that, for the present, at least, but little need be apprehended from the effect of natural causes Of deliberate acts of hostility as there could be no motive for such, there should be no apprehension on our part. We trust that, supported by the community of this city, and be tin state, the banks will be able to sir oio it all obstacles and on or . before the temh at day, to resume and maintain specie payments. The preparatory measures on their part þÿO Mieur to he first, a reduction of their liability s out of the state, and drawing in their foreign funds; socoin , an equalisation of the balances due from and to each other, and a mutual return of their notes, which may enable all to resume on an equal footing, and with equal safety; third, a sufficient increase oi then specie. On these points the committee will submit a separate report. ALBERT GALLATIN, PL PER STAGG, GEO. NEW BOLD, þÿCORN S. HEYER, JOHN I. PALMER, C. W. LAWRENCE, F. W. EDMONDS. Whereupon, the report was unanimously adopted by the meeting. On motion, Resolved, That the same be published. BENJ. M. BROWN, Chairman. Wm. M. Vkkmilye, Secretary. þÿA cwt York Com. Adv. March 2.

From the New York Express, January 27. NINE DAYS LATER FROM EUROPE. The packet ships, England, Capt. White, and Garkick, Capt. Palmer, arrived yesterday morning in company, having sailed from Liverpool 17th ult in company, but on account of the dense fog in the harbor, the England was not reported at so early an hour as the Garrick, though she was off the Hook the night before. The sailing of these two ships across the ocean is very remarkable. They sailed from this port in company, the England arriving off Liverpool about half a day in advance, and the passengers and the captains going up to the city together They arrived here in company, and the ships and passengers came up to this city in company, which is close sailing for 3000 miles out, and 3000 miles in.

From the Albany Argus, January 25. FROM THE IRONTIER. The scene of operations seems now to be transferred from Navy Island to the upper part of Lake Erie þÿ to Detroit, Maiden, Ac. Our latest advices from that quarter are via Toronto The Toronto Patriot of the 16th contains Detroit dates of the 12th, four days later than have been received from Detroit direct. The Detroit Post contains the official des- " brigadier general of the Patriot army, U. C. patches addressed by Th. J. Sutherland, " to "Gen. Van Ransselaer, commander-inchief," &c <fec., giving an account of the movements in that quarter. They are dated at Bois Blanc, U. C., on the 19th and 20th inst. The first despatch states that Sutherland found himself, on the 7th, " at the head of a very respectable and gallant force," with which on the 9th, he landed on the Bois Blanc Island, under the cover of the guns mounted on a sma'l schooner, captured the Island, pulled down the enemy's flag, and hoisted the Patriot tri color. The British force, consisting of about two hundred, principally negroes and Indians, fled on the first fire, leaving most of their camp equipage, a large quantity of ammunition, dec. The second despatch details the loss of the schooner with its three pieces of artillery, two sixes and one nine pounder, a small quantity of ammunition, and 3 persons including "Gen. Theller, Col. Dodge, and Captain Davis, of the infantry, and Col. Brophey, of the engineers." It seems that in the attempt to moor the schooner, so as to bring her guns

to bear upon a scow built sloop that was preparing, as was supposed, to attack Bois Island, she ran aground, parted her cable, and finally drifted over to the British side, and within gun shot of the force there, and was fired into until after she had surrendered. The despatches contain also, three Pro- " clamations." One addressed to the Patrio- " tic Citizens of Upper Canada," calling upon them to " rally around the standard of Liberty," and join the patriot forces in endeavor- A ing second to free " their To the land deluded supporters of Bri- " from tyranny," &c. þÿ tish tyranny in Upper Canada," requesting them to "lay down theii arms and return to their homes," to save themselves from the violence, and their " property from confiscation," &c.
FROM THE FRONTIER. If the statements in the letter following from Detroit, to the national Intelligencer, are confirmed, the war is over in that quar-

®AST33R T33!rajTXa33t »a®aamaw®3 AT33- I ter. þÿ but this Canada war is very like the Florida war, often over," but never ended : Detroit, Jan. 12, 1838. The capture of the Patriot schooner and Stores by the Canadians disconcerted all the plans of the invading army. They immediately retreated from Bois Blanc to an American island. Dissensions arose among them, and some of the officers withdrew from the service The extreme cold weather produced much suffering. Confidence was gone in the commanders, and the force has finally disbanded. Noihing remains but legal proceedings against those who have violated the law. þÿ All danger being now past, and the attempt to revolutionize Canada having been frustrated, the public officers begin to take measures for the preservation of their places. þÿ They assume the port and bearing of authority, and, doubtless, we shall be amused with the last act of their farce under the semblance of judicial proceedings. You may be assured, however, that most of our public officers are too far implicated in this matter to press very closely these prosecutions. Their remisness, at least, and the participation of some of them in the enterprise, have encouraged and sustained it. Nay, otherwise, it might have been crushed in its infancy. We shall probably be in an unsettled condition for a long time to come. Much ill feeling exists on both sides of the line. In Canada it is not without cause. A hostile force invading its territory, an armed ship sailing to and fro before its villages, and firing with

cannon shot into their dwellings, have given good reasons for exasperation on that side. Our authorities are proved to be entirely incompetent, if not unwilling, to maintain our neutrality ; and most surely they have manifested no very anxious wish to do so. A detachment of the United States Army ought to be stationed on this frontier forthwith ; nothing else, at present, will suffice. The next most important thing is a resolute and determined set of officers for the United States. þÿ For want of this, we have been nearly, if not quite, involved in war. Yours, &e.

From New Brunswick þÿ The British ship of the line Cornwallis, from the West Indies and Halifax, arrived at St. John on the 13th inst., with a portion of two regiments of regular troops. The 65th will remain here until next Monday, when two companies will proceed to Fredericton, there to be stationed for the present; about fifty men, with a captain and two subalterns, will remain in this garrison. The 93d Highlanders, we hear, may be daily expected here, on their route to Canada.

CITY AFFAIRS. Our friend Gilpin has removed his Reading Room to the new Merchant's Exchange on William street. The Room is one of the finest in the city. Mr. Gilpin is a most excellent and estimable citizen, attentive and persevering in his business, and every way deserving of the patronage of the public. The enclosure of " W. F. 1..," and several others, will be forwarded to "the Family in distress," whose case has deeply interested tiie public. Employment is needed.
MONEY. The mercantile community have never known r more pinching time than the present. The banks have got in nearly all their paper

and issue none, so that there is neither New York notes or specie to be had. The condition of things cannot apparently be þÿworse. A discussion is going on as to the resuming of specie þÿpayments, as to the manner and mode, nothing definite is fixed upon. By the law of this state, our banks must resume by the 10th of May, a period but little over 90 days. It would, however, seem impossible for our banks to resume unless the banks in Philadelphia united with them. The condition of Exchanges between this country and Europe is highly favorable to a resumption. The accounts by the " England" are highly favorable; cotton continued to advance ; money was abundant, and the balance of trade acknowledged to be decidedly against England.

EXCHA þÿNGE FOREIGN. The demand for remittances by the last packet, was not as great as that by the previous. The Dividends of the 1st of January having previously gone forward, the rate on London fell off about half per cent. Bills sold formerly at 109', a 110; France, 522; Holland, 401 ; Hamburg, 36 ; Bremen 81 a 81 J. It is impossible to predict what the rate of Exchange will range at, but from the large quantity of Cotton now going forw ard, and the advance of price, there is a fair prospect that the rate will not advance, but rathe fall off.

From the Albany Argus. From the West. þÿ Only one of the three mails due yesterday, arrived. The Buffalo papers are of Thursday last. The Star of that date says : þÿ A rumor very much like the truth, has reached this city, that official news lias been received by Col. Mc'Nab that Duncombe had taken Maiden, and on other towns on the western frontier of Canada, and was making rapid progress, with nearly 2000 men, well armed. If this be true, which wo have very little reason to doubt, the seat of war will soon return to the Niagara frontier. Mac Nab w ill have only got rid of Van Rensselaer, for a season to be met by both Don Combe & Van Rensselaer, in such a position that he will be obliged to fight or run. There are many rumors connected with the above, and other matters relating to ('anada. One is, that tire Patriots on the borders of Lake Siincoe, near Toronto, have risen in some force, seized the arsenal of the North West Fur Company, and are marching upon Toronto. An Express had reached the Government house at Toronto, with despatches to the effect that Duncombe, with 300 men and some pieces of cannon from Detroit, had taken possession of the Island of Bois Blanc, as has been already mentioned. And to balance these accounts, is another by an express at Kingston, from the London district, signed by John B Askin, stating that a detachment of royalist boats had succeeded in capturing, after a short engagement, near Maiden, a schooner with 400 stand of arms, 3 pieces cannon, of and an abundance of am-

munition on þÿboard the number of men not mentioned, but it is stated that the schooner lost one killed, 8 wounded and 12 prisoners. The Caroline þÿ Mr. Wells, the proprietor of this illfated boat, now the subject of so much and so important controversy, called at our office this morning, to state the following facts :

The Caroline was never bought, chartered, hired, or bonded in any manner by the people on Navy Island, or any persons in their interest She was started by himself as a matter of speculation, to run as a ferry boat between Black Kock, Tonawanda, Schlosser, and Navy Island, for freight or passage. She had her regular papers. She carried no flag but the flag of the United States, and had no other on board. We learn, incidentally, from a gentleman in Buffalo who has taken passage on board of the steam boat New England, for Cleveland, that that boat will leave Buffalo this morning. Her movement is connected with the movement of those who have left Navy Island. The greater part of Gen. Burt's Brigade of infantry, and Gen. Randall's Brigade of Artillery, have volunteered their services to Gen. Scott for three months, and been accepted. One hundred and ten U S. soldiers arrived at Buffalo on Wednesday evening.

From the Kingston (U. C.) Herald, Jan. 10. The traveller brings the accounts of a gallant action at Amhcrstburgh. A gang of pirates robbed the arsenal at Detroit, loaded a schooner with the spoils, and sailed to Amherstburgh, and fired on the town. The inhabitants had no arms, but they collected in the night armed with pitchforks, and whatever came to hand. They then attacked and captured the schooner, killing one man, and taking 12 prisoners, with 300 stand of arms, 3 cannon, and a large supply ol the munitions of war Thus in every quarter defeat and ruin wait on the rebels and pirates.

a A»aK jrasTan® asz_m-jroaa3mr® 8 Ataa Interview with the pope. þÿ The following interesting account of an interview with his Holiness the present Pope is extracted from a private letter, written by D. S , a medical gentleman, in September, 1835, to his friends in Scotland. It will amply repay perusal ; þÿ " To-day we had a private interview with his Holiness þÿ nay you must not laugh for I assure you of the fact t and, although I did not kiss his toe, got his blessing. As I you will be curious to know the manner of the Court, I shall be a little particular. Mr. J n knew an Englishman, who is a Count of the Pope's making, and a private friend, arid we managed it through him. A letter was sent to the Lord High Chamberlain, containing the request for an audience, and last night his Lordship returned an answer appointing to-day before 12 for the purpose.-- When the letter arrived, 1 was at the house of an Irishman, a patient of mine for the time being, and we were all in a bustle. We were obliged to go in a court dress to wit, þÿ kneebreeches, black silk stockings, and shoe, buckles. We had nothing prepared, when, to my relief, our Irish friend said that he had a pair that had never been on but once, when he was presented, and he begged I would use them, as also his stockings and buckles þÿ and they fitted admirably ; but poor M r. J n had the misfortune of being six feet three, so that it was impossible to get either breeches or stockings. It was eventually agreed that he should go in long clothes, and that an explanation should be given to the

Chamberlain. We set out this morning for the palace with our friend the Count, and went through four splendid rooms, containing the Swiss Guards in their old grotesque uniforms, and the Officers of the Court ; when we arrived in the ante chamber, where we found Monsignor Fieschie, the Lord High Chamberlain, who received us with great kindness, and talked with us for about half an hour. The Governor of Rome, who was also waiting, was called in with his papers, and when he returned wc were next sent for. þÿ On entering the presence chamber we knelt on one knee, and then walked up to his Holiness, and knelt down once more, and our friend kissed the Pope's toe. Upon his rising, his Holiness entered, with the greatest kindness and cheerfulness, into conversation. He is a fine-looking old man, about 60; amidst all the splendour of royalty, retains all the kindness and gentleness that characterized him when he was only a monk. lie talked to Mr. J n about banking, and was very witty in his remarks. The Court had got a bank established for its own convenience, but had drawn too hard upon it, and the proprietors at length declined to make further advances. þÿ Mr. J. n said his bank had an unlimited capital, and his Holiness replied that was the right sort of bank, but as for the Roman bank, he thought it would soon bo bank rupt. This excited a deal of merriment, Mr. J n recommended saving-banks as an excellent means of improving the condition of the people ; and his Holiness said,

'Oh, as for that, we don't feci the want of money, as we Romans live mostly on memorials !' (alluding to the manner in which he is pestered with petitions for money.) I was next introduced as the writer of a medical work ; and his Holiness said, What is it on ' þÿ cholera V The count answered that it was not. The Pope then said he had received about forty volumes on the cholera from diflereat medical roe n j and that one Was sent

from Vienna the other day with a hnte eafti estly recommending him to try the remedy it advocated, which consisted in washing thd body over with oil and vinegar. His Holiness said it was not a had receipt ; but it only wanted a little salt to make a salid of him ! þÿ There was no withstanding this sally, and we all became uproarious. Only a few words more passed He said he would feel exceedinerly J obliged O a O if I could cure his Secretary of State, who is ill of the gout ; so that it is very probable I may pay him a visit. We knelt down, and received his þÿbenediction. He laid his hands on our heads, and we then left him exceedingly delighted with our interview, The audience chamber is a plaid room, with a crimson velvet canopy, under wiiich was placed a table with writing matelials, at which his Holiness was transacting business, and a chair. He was dressed in a close gown of white flannel, perfectly plain, and stood all the time." þÿ had a small white cap on his head, and Edinburgh Chronicle .

A Remarkable Fact. þÿ Some late experiments by M. Namais, of Vienna, on the blood of persons who have died of cholera, proves that there exists a deadly poison in it. He drew a portion of the blood from the heart of a person who died of this disease, and inserted it through an incision of the skin of a rabbit, live days after the animal became dejected, and o»> the tenth day died. The blood in its heart was found black and gramons. The blood of this rabbit was introduced under the skin of another, which caused its death in twenty four hours. Tlx; same phenomena attended the dissection of this as those of the other rabbit It was desirable now to know whether the blood of patients dead from other diseases would produce similar effects The doctor then inserted the black foetid blood of a person dead from intestinal gangrene, under the skin of a rabbit, but the health of the rabbit wus got affected ! þÿ There, was a similar result following the injection of the blood of a person who had died of an aneurism. Others will draw their infefences from these facts.

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, January 31 1838. Bank Committee. The committee from the New York banks, who visited Philadelphia last week, have returned. We are not furnished with the result of their deliberations ; but this we believe, that notwithstanding the talk in New York about specie payments, they neither can pay nor wish to pay specie. How can they ? þÿ There are payable in New \ork within about sixty days, four millions of dollars in bonds. Now if the genera! government will take only specie or treasury notes, how are the New Yorkers to meet that payment, which is nearly equal to all the specie in the whole of that state? When people talk about resuming specie payment, let them think a little of the causes of suspension, and of the ruinous consequences of a re suspension. While the government persists in its war upon the people by the demand of specie, it is impossible for any one to say when specie payments can be permanently resumed.

Lower Canada. þÿ We have the Montreal papers of the 25th inst. The members the of executive council were expected at Montreal, from Quebec, to attend upon Sir John Colborne and organize the government anew, under his administration. The following extracts are from the Transcript The rumors which had been for some days current, and which for obvious reasons we refrained from noticing, have not only continued to circulate, but have produced their effect ; and the French Canadian population have been leaving the city and island of Montreal, for several days past. We are far from wishing unnecessarily to denounce them, or wantonly to wound their feelings ; but certainly there is in this something rery remarkable, something which seems to demand explanation While the British population are, one and all, in a state of the utmost tranquility and confidence, this sudden bustle and confusion of French departure bespeaks on their part a remarkable timidity ; or it indicates a knowledge, an expectation of some intended outbreak, which inducts them to separate themselves from their British fellow colonists, & to retire from what they suppose to be the field of approaching contest. þÿ Some satisfactory explanation is due to their own þÿcharacter and we look for it accordingly. Flood in Montreal. þÿ On Sunday, the 2 1 st instant, Montreal was visited by an in-

ZDAIT33& TjBSKTJSTBaSX undation greater than has been known by the oldest inhabitants of that city. The south part of the city, and its suburbs, were covered with water varying from two to eight feet. In the neighborhood of the ship yards, the water was so high, that the large steamboat Victoria, which plies between Montreal and Laprairie, and two other vessels, were floated off the slocks. Commissioners street, Point a Calliere, Mc'Gill, and St. Paul's streets, had to be navigated in boats and canoes ; the latter street is the chief place of business, and it is said a large amount of property has been destroyed. At the latest advices, the water had frozen þÿ consequently the difficulty of removing merchandize and furniture was very great, having to be cut out from the ice. In the low grounds about Griffentown and the neighboring suburbs, it has been attended with great loss of cattle. A meeting of the citizens of Montreal has been held, for the purpose of raising funds to relieve those in immediate distress.

Correspondence of Commercial Advertiser. Dunkirk, Jan. 23, 1838. I have been a constant reader of your paper for more than thirty years, and never have I been more satisfied with the course taken by it than since the commencement of the excitement on this frontier, growing out of the Canada rebellion. Yesterday Col Worth arrived here in the steamboat Fulton, with a force of about 200 men, accompanied by the deputy marshal and other civil authorities. He debarked about 150 of his troops and marched immediately to Fredonia, where the marshal took posession of some two or three hundred muskets, &c., which were put into five wagons, brought to this place, and secured on board the steamboat. Some two or three hundred of these misguided men have been in this vicinity, waiting for a boat ; and when it was known t hat the Fulton was in the service of ihe United States, nothing could exceed their disappointment. Col. Worth, having heard, while here, of some recent movements by the insurgents

ATJI3 and their abetters, near Maiden, made all haste to reach that vicinity before the ice should prevent him. This morning the New England, with a detachment under command of Major Young, U. S. A., came into the harbor, and has left a guard to protect the peaceable citizens from the depredations of these roving marauders, and to aid the civil authorities in securing any munitions of war that may be found. In this region the energy of General Scott has put an end to their operations ; at the West they have lost the arms plundered from the arsenals, and cannot, 1 think, be much longer deceived by their unprincipled leaders. Patriotism was their profession, but plunder was their real object; and every lover of peace and of the laws will sanction the course pursued by the commander in-chief to enforce our neutrality. There has been very little excitement here. The larger part of the population have been sound, and the most bawling ' patriots" have been office-holders under the general government. Not more than 50 of the 500 on Navy Island came from Canada þÿ 'Ihe matter is now undoubtedly ended, but the cost is yet to come, and it will not be a trifle.

From the London Times of December U5lh. Had the proposition been put to us four or five years ago, to fling Lower Canada overboard altogether, as a dependency more expensive and troublesome than beneficial, we hardly know what our answer might have been, always securing the rights and interests, and consulting the inclinations, of our dear native countrymen in the Upper Province, and retaining the single fortress of Quebec. Now the lime has gone past for such discussion. The national honor is involved in the necessity of crushing this wanton and audacious attack on the integrity of the realm. The rebellion of Lower Canada must be put down> or rebellion will not be confined to the western shores of the Atlantic. proceedings of tiie british parliament. The Express of this city has over and over again assured its readers, that the insurgents ol Canada would find encouragement and support in Great Britain þÿ advocates in the two houses of Parliament þÿ and in the Government itself a disposition to leave the colonies to their fate, without assistance or support. How well the Express understands the feelings of the English people, and the policy of the English Government, is amply demonstrated by the following report of proceedings in

the House ol Commons, on the arrival of intelligence from Lower Canada, that resistance to the constituted authorities had already broken out in violence and bloodshed The truth is, that npy sign of weakness or indecision in relation to the maintenance of the

Cann das, on the part of the ministry, would oust the Whigs from power more certainly and quickly than almost any other political error they could fall into. HOUSE OF COMMONS þÿ Dec. 23. adjournment. Lord J. Russei.i, moved that the house, at its rising, do adjourn to Tuesday, the 16th January. Lord George Bentinck said that he did not think it right to sleep over the Christmas holidays. He thought it would be more becoming that house to support the government in any strong measures which they might adopt with reference to Canada. He therefore moved, as an amendment, that the house should adjourn to Thursday next, the 28th day of December. The house then divided þÿ For the original motion 44 Against it 7 Majority against the amendment þÿ CANADA . 37 Lord J. Russei.l gave notice that from and after the 16th of January he should move that the consideration of the affairs of Canada have precedence till Feb. 1st ; and that on the 16th January he should move that part of her majesty's speech which referred to Canada should be considered. Lord J. RusselL, in moving the order of the day regarding supply, said þÿ I do so thus early for the purpose of giving the hon. gentleman, the member for Westminster, (Mr. Leader,) an opportunity of making any remarks that to him may seem necessary or expedient on the subject of the affairs of Canada ; but lest the hon gentleman should have been misled by the intention declared by me in this house, I wish now to state to the hon gentle-

man, and to this house, what my intentions at present are with respect to adjournment. þÿ It was intended and I thought I should have been enabled, to move an adjournment to the 1st of February, with a view to postpone the business of the house to that period ; but, in considering the whole question of the affairs of Canada, I shall not think that 1 am discharging my duty, or that 1 am justified in now proposing so long an adjournment þÿ (hear, hear.) 1 have already stated that, although Lord Gosford declared his willingness to remain in Canada as long as the necessities of the government required it, yet it was his lordship's wish to resign his government when he found that there was no longer a prospect of a reconciliation being effected. According to þÿ that wish, 1 have informed the house that the government immediately relieved Lord Gosford from his duty, and committed the temporary government of Lower Canada to Sir John Colborne. Such being the state of things, although I do not believe that any remedy which might be applied by Parliament would give a greater authority than has already been entrusted to Sir John Colborne, yet I do say that I think we should not be justified, when we have the means of assembling Parliament in considerable numbers, to delay that assembling of Parliament for any long þÿperiod that we ought bring to Parliament together as soon as it can be done in any considerable number, in order that on the course to be pursued, either in respect to what has lately taken place, or upon what may be the intelligence between this time and the re assembling of the house the judgement of Parliament may be pronounced þÿ (hear ) Therefore I beg leave to state now, that it is our intention, in the first place, to produce to-morrow all the information that can be presented without injury to tlie public service, collected from the despatches and information

He must say that, if he were to discuss that question, he did not know what conclusion it might lead to, for he did not know why that argument might not be applied to the united kingdom. It had been said that the present question was the same as that which caused the Ame rican war. America did not desire to avoid contributing to the expenses of the government, but they

denied the right of the British Parliament to tax them by the stamp act without their own consent ; and this was the reason that Lord Chatham had called the act oppressive, because the consent of the American people had not been asked. But was this the case with Canada ? No, the story of Canada was widely different. In the year 1791 the constitution of Canada was settled, and an a»scmbly was established to be elected by the people.

ttcwutenvrm This country did not attempt to tax the Canadians, hut left that power to their own legislative assembly, and also the disposal of the revenue arising from those taxes. This country never pretended to tax them, or dispose of their taxes. What the Canadians demanded was, that the -legislative council should be elected as well as the assembly, and that all persons holding public offices, should be removable at pleasure. Because, then, their demands were not granted, they refused the supplies and stopped the machinery of government The act of her majesty's ministers was, therefore a defensive act, to prevent the machinery of the Canadian government from being entirely put an end to. Even if they were to grant the demands made upon them, he did not think it would secure the peace and harmony of the colony. Suppose the legislativecoune.il to be elective, and a bill introduced into the legislative assembly for preventing troops from entering Quebec or Montreal, and it was agreed to by a council so constituted, what remedy would remain ? The governor, it is true, might refuse his assent to such a bill, but might not the two assemblies refuse the supplies, as bad been done before, and what remedy would then remain ? The machinery, of government must necessarily be stopped until the commands were complied with. They would refuse the supplies, on the ground that no troops ought to be sent to those places. Their position as regarded Canada now, and as regarded the United States at a former period, was, there-

fore, as unlike as anv two things could be. þÿ When the resolution passed that house last session, he did not in lulge in decided predilections. It was not his habit to do so. Speech of the King of the French at the opening of the Chambers. þÿ Peers and Deputies. þÿ France is free and tranquil, her prosperity is rapidly increasing, her institutions are being consolidated, and her confidence in their stability is increasing. þÿ The re-establishment of the empire of the laws has permitted me to follow the impulse of my heart A great act, the recollection of which will ever be dear to me, the amnesty, has testified the strength of mv government. It has calmed the public mind, weakened the influence of evil passions, and has daily and still more isolated plans of disorder. þÿ I have desired to see the electoral colleges assembled. My confidence in the country has not been deceived ; I shall meet with from you that loyal support afforded to me by the chambers for seven years, to ensure to France the blessings of order and peace. þÿ I have only to congratulate myself on my relations with all the foreign powers, and never has the general peace appeared to me more firmly secured. þÿ Nevertheless civil war still desolates the peninsula. The Queen Regent supports with courage and perseverance the rights of her august daughter, Queen Isabella II. 1 continue to execute faithfully the clauses of the quadruple treaty, and 1 have reason to hope for the success of a cause which has all our sympathies þÿ The marriage of the eldest of my sons has completed my wishes. With the recollection of this event, which is the source of much happiness for my family, will always

be connected that of the testimonies of affection with which France, the chambers, and the inhabitants of this capital, surrounded the young princess who became one of my children. þÿ second My daughter, the Princess Mary, has since contracted an alliance which will add to our relations of amity with heighboring states. þÿ In Africa our expectations have been fulfilled. The French flag floats on the walls of Constantine. If victory has sometimes done more for the power of France, it has never exalted to a higher point the glory and the honor of her arms. My son the Duke of Nemours, has borne his share in the peril. þÿ 11 is young brother wished to join him, and to participate in that community of toil and danger which has long identified my sons with the army. Their blood belongs to France as well as that of all her children þÿ (loud and continued cheering.) þÿ In addressing thanks to Heaven for the protection granted to our arms, I have to deplore with you the loss of many brave men, who have perished on the field of honor. þÿ þÿ The country surrounds their tombs with her regret and her gratitude She has ratified beforehand all that I have ordered to satisfy the public grief, and discharge, the debt due by France to her heroic supporters. A bill -will be presented to you for granting to the widow and children of the brave Gen. Damremont a testimony of the national gratitude. I have exalted to the first dignity of the army the aged warrior who has replaced him, and
who staled that in his lengthened career he bad seen nothing which had not been equalled by our young soldiers.

JBAW33E T33T1W3»-J33t tO&aatfctJT&a A'TJ3> þÿ In the east of Algiers, as well as in the west, I have desired peace, but the obstinacy ot the Bey who commanded at Constantine, has compelled us to prove once more to the natives of our possessions in Africa, that they must abandon the idea of resisting us. In the west a convention has been concluded, the conditions of which are being faithfully executed, and fortunate results have been already derived from it. þÿ A faithful report of our situation in Africa shall be presented to you, and 1 shall have to demand of you the means of providing for the wants of our establishments. þÿ Our naval squadrons every where afford to our commercial relations the support and protection which can be expected from them. Envoys have been sent from our ports to remove the difficulties so long opposed to the execution of the engagements entered into by Hayti toward France. At the same time some naval forces are directing their course toward the coast of Mexico, to ensure to the French who trade in the interior of those countries the justice and the security to which they are entitled þÿ I have concluded a treaty of commerce with the Bolivians, and 1 hope that we shall establish successively with all the states of Sou h America such relations as may be beneficial to our commerce. þÿ The situation of our finances is still prosperous, and the public revenue has been still farther increased since last session. þÿ The bills announced for the article 69 of the charter shall be again presented.

þÿ Our penitentiary system has long called for all the attention of my government, and you will have to examine a bill for its improvement. þÿ The object of another bill will be the reform of our legislation with regard to commercial societies. þÿ Considerable funds have been already voted for the public works. It remains for you to bring to perfection our great lines of communication, and to create new ones to facilitate the progress of the ever-increasing produce of our agriculture and our industry. Some general views forming a united whole will be presented to you on this important subject, together with the detailed plans of several undertakings of great consequence. þÿ I have never been surrounded by the chamber under more favorable circumstances. Let us preserve, gentlemen, by our union and our wisdom, what we have acquired by our courage and patriotism. Let us endeavor to efface the painful recollections of all our dissensions, and of the agitations from which we have suffered so much : let the only trace left be a feeling of the necessity of preventing their return. Let us persist, gentlemen, in that regular and peaceable course to which we owe the increase of the wealth and prosperity which France now enjoys. This is the dearest wish of my heart. My life is devoted to the maintenance of all the guarantees of our repose and our liberties, and it is to accomplish this grand task that I claim your support." «< From the Philadelphia Public Ledger, Jan. 30

Evening Fost. þÿ brief description of its various parts we copy þÿ It is 22 feet long and contains 26 cubic feet hydrogen, and 29 cubic feet, 56 inches atmospheric air, contained in strong metal boxes secured under the decks and thwarts.
