THE STEAMERS. It is with much regret we are informed that both the Steamers ( City of kingston and Sir Lionel Smith) are about to proceed to New-York immediately for the purpose of being repaired, each vessel having been on shore, notwithstanding their having Pilots on board ; and, although it appears that very little injury has been sustained by either, further than some to their false keels and copper, yet, to allow them to remain any longer in their present condition, exposed to the descriptive ravages of that worm, in the West India seas, which quickly destroys all timber unprotected by copper, would be dangerous, Since these vessels have been on the station, they have been of the greatest utility to the inhabitants. Friends have met friends, who only know each other by correspondence ; and aged persons have been enabled to visit each other, who from their infirm state, would never have been able to travel

ADDRESS From the members of the British Constitutional Society of Upper Canada to the citizens of the United States. Every American must by this time be fully aware that in the beginning of last December an insurrection broke out in the province of Upper Canada. The insurgents, who were acting in concert with the French party in Lower Canada, had nearly succeeded in surprising the defenceless city of Toronto, but on the alarm being given were compelled to retreat ; and in a few days both in the Home and London Districts, to which portions of the province the rebellion was confined, the insurgents had either hastily dispersed, or surrendered themselves as prisoners on the ap proach of the loyal militia. Their utmost number, including all who appeared in arms against the government in both districts, never exceeded one thousand, while ten thousand men voluntarily repaired toToionto, directly the news of its being invested by a rebel force was spread through the country ; and additional thousands þÿw ere daily pouring in to the defence of our metropolis, until the Lieutenant Governor issued a proclamation declaring that the insurrection had been quelled, and that further assistance was unnecessarv. In the London District a similar result followed on the revolutionary outbreak in that quarter. The persons who thus rose up in resistance to the constituted authorities were, w ith a few exceptions, either worthless characters, or

blind dupes of their leader William Lyon Mackenzie. They were reduced to submission, not by the þÿQueen stroops, (for there was not a British soldier in the whole province) but by the undisciplined inhabitants of the country, who rose in one mass to confound their treasonable designs. The question, ao you wish to change your Jorm of government and become a republic ? was fairly put to the people. The people, unawed by military force, and exercising an uufettered will, decided in the negative by an overwhelming majority. Defeated in his first attempt, Mackenzie succeeded in reaching the lerritorv of the United States. The citizens of Buffalo received him with open arms þÿ sympathies! with him as if he had been a Tell, a Wallace, a Washington, ora Hiogo; and furnished him with the means of waging war against tlie British government in Upper Canada Since then, it must be notorious to you all, he has taken possession of Navy Island, which lies in the Niagara river, about two miles above the falls, and which forms a portion of the British territory. To fortify this spot, he has broken into the public arsenals at Buffalo and Batavia, and carried off several stands of arms and other munitions of war. The proper authorities of the state of New York have demanded these arms from him, and he has refused to restore them Moreover, we regret to add, several hundred armed American citizens have joined him on the Island, and fresh numbers are daily crowding to bis aseistance, and consequently invading our soil.

In addition to these hostile ads on the part Of your fellow citizens, they have made prisoners of some British subjects, and fired upon the British forces from Grand Island, w hich is situated within your territory, as well as upon a boat bearing the British flag from your main land near Fort Schlosscr. This act, so conformable to the dictates of self preservation and self defence, and so accordant with the principles and practice of international law, has been artfully made use of by designing men to assist them in kindling a war between the British Government and the UnHed States. The grossest misstatements have been industriously circulated, and no artifice left untried that could have the slightest effect in inflaming your passions against us your Canadian neighbors, Humors, confiimed by the tone of several of your journals, daily reach us, that an act of selfdefence on our part has been misconstrued into a wanton, hostile aggression þÿ that meetings have been field to assist the Patriots, (so the rebels who have been guilty of murder, arson and robbery, and have deliberately fired at women, have been ridiculously termed,) þÿ that armed bodies of American citizens are being organized with the intention of marching to the frontier, invading our province, and annexing it to the United Slates. Such is our present relative position þÿ What was it two short months ago? Every

We travelled through your country and beheld your growing prosperity witli satisfaction; you visited us, and we felt gratified at being the objects of your kindly curiosity. No inconsiderable commerce was carried on between us our knowledge of English literature was þÿ almost entirely derived through your pressþÿ such of your laws as were adapted to our situation and did not clash with the princi pies of our institutions, we gladly borrowed from you, and incorporated into our Provincial Statute Book: and though you still preferred your republic and we our monarchy, yet sprung from tlie same lineage, arid speaking the same language, we lived on a footing of harmony and good will. The late and passing events to which we already have alluded in brief, threaten to interrupt the continuance of this happy understanding. William Lay on Mackenzie, an unprincipled adventurer, who has long harassed our province with turbulence and sedition, and retarded tlie cause of real reform by tlie propagation of lawless and revolutionary doctrines, who has checked the influx of emigration, and whose silence, nay, whose support, might long since have been purchased by our local government, had it been base enough to entertain the wish, þÿ

CONSTANTINE. (From the Landscape Annual) The town of Constantine is almost three times as large as Algiers, and is surrounded with strong walls, more than thirty five feet high. Founded during the early aehiev ments of the Carthaginians, it owed its vast population and its unequalled embellishments to the splendid reign of Massanissa We are assured by Strabo, that it first subdued the JVlassouglians who cultivated the fruitful plain of Hainsah. Scipio Emilanus extended the ancient kingdom of Massanissa and Mccissa bv the addition of the valley of Bragado, when it took the name of Numidia. It Was desolated by the wars of Marius and of Scylla, the oppressions of the old Roman Proconsuls, and by repeated civil strife. þÿ Aemissal, vanquished by Cseser at Thepsa, with Cato and Lahietius, lost apaitof his kingdom: but he re-established his fortunes by the trade he carried on with tin' interior of Africa. Towards the year 45 of the Christian era Numidia became a Roman province. It was governed by Proconsuls ; and after the time of Dioclesiau by Presidents, under the orders, it is stated, of a Vicar at Carthage; subsequently by the Prefect of the Italian Pretorium : and was placed in the military division of a Count residing at Bona, who had between 2,000 and 0,000 troops quartered in a great number of fortresses and castles tinder his command. Numidia embraced the Christian faith but it was torn bv persecutions, toy dissensions, heresies between the I >onalists and the Arians. The houses and furni-

ture of the Catholics became the prey of the former, who also burnt Cirtlia. Between the years 340 and 350, the town was rebuilt by the Emperor Constantine, from whom it acquired its modern name The position of Constantine is very formidable : the Romans fortified it with an enclosure of lofty walls flanked at intervals with strong towers. The enclosure is still in good preservation. In Pliny's time the city stood on a kind of lofty promontory inaccessible on every side, except, towards the south-east. þÿ The town inclined a little to the south, and was terminated to the north by a precipice of <500 feet 'in depth. The view is here magnificent, stretching far over a series of valleys at one period covered with country seats, palaces, and Koman villas, of which numerous vestiges are yet to be seen. Again, to the east, it is commanded by lofty mountains, connected by a chain of almost inaccessible rocks. Besides the general traces of diversity of ruins scattered all over, we have still remaining, near the centre of the city, those capacious cisterns which received the waters brought thither from Physgeah by an immense aqueduct, great part of which, showing jt to have been very sumptuous, still remains. The cisterns which are about twenty in number, make an area of fifty yards square. One of the gates is of a beautiful reddish stone, not inferior to polished marble, and the pillars are neatly moulded in panels. An altar of pure white marble forms part of a neighbour-

ing wall, and the side in view presents us with u well-shaped sumpelum in bold relief. The gate towards the south-east is erected oa a similar plan, only much smaller, and lies open to a bridge that was built over this port of the valley. This was indeed a mustor-picce of its kind ; the gailery and columns

The elephants, facing each other twist their trunks together, and the lady who appears dressed in her own hair, with a close bodied garment liken þÿlady s riding-habit of our times, raises up her peticoat with her right hand, and looks scornfully upon the city Among the ruins to the southwest of the bridge is the greatest part of a triumphal arch, called Gasser Goulah, or as it is interpreted the þÿ Castle of the þÿGiant, composed of three arches of which that in the centre, as usual is the most spacious All the mouldings and friezings are curiously embellished with the figures of flowers, battle axes, and other ornament. The Corinthian pilasters, erected on each side of the grand arch, are panelled, like the gates of the city, in a style peculiar to Cirtlia. Beyond the precints of the city, under the great precipice numerous sepulchral inscriptions are to be seen. In the fearful days of the Vandals, Constantine suffered from the devastations of t hat ferocious power; though it preserved, till the yet more sweeping conquest of the Arabs, those municipal light and laws conferred by the Carthaginian trader and the Roman colonizer. This city was slow to receive the Ma-

iiomedan doctrines which it only adopted with Numidia and the rest of Africa in 710. It once formed part of the kingdom of Africa, under the dynasty of the Fatirnites till the year 9(i0. It then passed under the dominion of the Zervtcs. who reigned at Taburt and at þÿAsch vr over the territory of the eastern division, which afterwards became gtlie Regency of Algiers. After a lapse of six hundred years of variable fortune under the Almoravides and the Almohadcs, the city fell under the leaden sceptre of the Osmanlis in 1550. The cultivation of the þÿsoil the most productive in Africa þÿ an industrious population, Commerce with central Africa and an advantageous position between the Desert and the best portion of the date country, the most fertile part of the kingdom of Tunis þÿ that of Sousah, and chiefly subject to the dominion of the Divan of þÿUgtcrs have given to Constantine a considerable degree of importance under the predatory rule of the Turk. Its commercial connexions were principally with Tunis, and were so injurious to the Algerines, that war was declared by them with Tunis in 1782 and 1783. Some inconsiderable hostilities were followed by the plague in 1784. Between both these terrific scourges a great portion of the population of these dominions was swept away. Previous to 1780 the inhabitants of this spacious city amounted to nearly fifty thousand souls ; but has subsequently declined to little more than half that number. A monthly caravan used formerly

to set out for Tunis þÿ A wealthy cargo, estimated at no less than one hundred thousand Spanish piasters, or six million six hundred thousand francs yearly. It also carried on trade with Bonn, the Beys of Quol and Stora, and with the Roral African Company of Mar seilles.
